meta.blurb: Maya finds a box of handwritten recipe cards in her grandmother's bakery, and her uncle says every living thing has one. Over one summer, he shows her how genes are copied, why mistakes happen, and why genes are not puppet strings.
meta.bible: Maya: a curious girl of about twelve who helps in her grandmother's bakery for the summer. Teo: her uncle, a biology teacher, patient and funny. Rosa: Maya's grandmother, who owns the Bakery and keeps an old Recipe box of handwritten cards. The whole book is Maya and Teo talking in the bakery over one summer, using the Recipe box as a picture of how Genes work. Real facts used: DNA is a long molecule with four letters, A, C, G and T; a human cell holds about 3 billion letters and about 20,000 Genes; humans have 23 pairs of Chromosomes; Gregor Mendel studied Pea plants in the 1860s; any two people share nearly all of their DNA; Humans and Chimpanzees share more than 98 out of 100 letters; about eight in every hundred letters of human DNA came from ancient Viruses; a gene tool called CRISPR was invented in 2012 and a treatment using it for sickle cell disease was approved in 2023. Key terms: Protein, Amino acids, Haemoglobin, Mutation, Nucleus, Genome, Cell, Bacteria, Antibiotic, Malaria, Lactase, Hox, EPAS1, Phenylketonuria, Natural selection, Darwin, Meiosis, Cuckoo, Bat, Queen, Worker. Voice: friendly, curious and clear; genes never "want" or "think", and the book says so; science is real and hedged where scientists disagree; no invented numbers, studies or quotes. Added for the full-length book: Elena: Maya's mother, Rosa's daughter and Teo's sister, who works abroad for the summer and phones on Sundays. Carmen: Rosa's younger sister, who keeps her own copy of the family cake card. Dario: a friendly man who delivers the flour and keeps Bees on a hill outside town. Ines: a nurse who buys bread every morning and has identical twin sons, Leo and Nico, aged nine. Bernardo: the name Rosa gives her old sourdough starter, a jar of Yeast and Bacteria kept alive for years. The bakery has a notebook that Maya keeps, a doorframe in the pantry with pencil marks of the family's heights, and a wall of family photographs. The summer runs from early June to the first week of September, and Maya is twelve. Teo shows ideas with flour, ribbons, cards and cups on the counter. More key terms: DNA, RNA, Enzyme, Ribosome, Helix, Histone, Histones, Chromosome, Chromosomes, Molecule, Codon, Amylase, Collagen, Keratin, Fungus, Fungi, Yeast, Mendel, Brno, Monastery, Allele, Alleles, Heritability, Replication, Polymerase, Proofreading, Frameshift, Ultraviolet, Penicillin, Fleming, Galapagos, Finches, Superbug, Mitochondria, Plasmid, Retrovirus, Retroviruses, Transposon, McClintock, Neanderthal, Neanderthals, Denisovans, Anaemia, Mosquito, Mosquitoes, Plasmodium, Lactose, Himalaya, Andes, Meiosis, Zygote, Embryo, Placenta, Hamilton, Trivers, Warbler, Warblers, Drones, Roost, Weaning, Van Valen, Carroll, Epigenetic, Phenylalanine, Teosinte, Brassica, Belyaev, Siberia, CRISPR, Cas9, Casgevy, Genome, Genomes, Sequencing, Humpback, LUCA, Yoghurt. People named in the text (all long past or unnamed in detail): Rosalind Franklin (X-ray photographs of DNA, helped to show the double spiral in 1953 in Cambridge), Gregor Mendel (peas, Brno, 1866, died 1884, rediscovered about 1900), Alexander Fleming (1928 mould that killed bacteria, penicillin), Barbara McClintock (jumping genes in maize, 1940s, Nobel Prize 1983), William Hamilton (1964, helping relatives), Leigh Van Valen (1973, Red Queen) and Lewis Carroll (Through the Looking-Glass), Dmitri Belyaev (tame foxes in Siberia from 1959). Places: Florida (pale beach mice), Galapagos Islands (finches, drought of 1977), New Zealand lakes (snails and parasites), Siberia, the Pacific Ocean. More facts used: a human cell copies its DNA with about one mistake in a billion letters after proofreading and repair; about two million red blood cells are made every second; the Earth is about four and a half billion years old and life is at least three billion; Homo sapiens is about three hundred thousand years old; people outside Africa carry about one or two letters in a hundred from Neanderthals; bread wheat has forty-two chromosomes; a worm and rice have about as many or more genes than a person; a CRISPR treatment for sickle cell disease was approved in 2023. The book ends with Maya writing her own recipe card and Teo calling her a new edition of an old book.

beats.scene: Maya opens an old wooden box of handwritten recipe cards in the bakery
beats.summary: Maya finds her grandmother's old recipe box, and her uncle Teo says every living thing has one.

beats.scene: Rosa wipes her floury hands and shows Maya a faded card
beats.summary: Rosa says the box belonged to her mother, and the cards were copied by hand over many years.

beats.scene: Teo and Maya lean on the flour-dusted counter with an empty notebook
beats.summary: Teo promises that if Maya asks one question a day while they work, she will understand the box by the end of summer.

beats.scene: Teo holds up one recipe card beside a bowl of flour and eggs
beats.summary: A recipe card is a set of instructions, and a gene is also a set of instructions.

beats.scene: A baker's card for plain bread lists flour, water, salt and yeast in order
beats.summary: A recipe is a list of steps in a fixed order, and the order matters as much as the ingredients.

beats.scene: Two loaves from one recipe sit side by side, one darker
beats.summary: The same card can give slightly different loaves, because baking also depends on the oven, the air and the baker's hands.

beats.scene: A cell shown as a small busy kitchen with workers and a recipe box
beats.summary: Every cell is a tiny kitchen, and almost every cell keeps a full copy of the recipe box.

beats.scene: Rosa locks the old box in the bakery office and photocopies one card
beats.summary: The original cards stay safe in an office, and the cooks work from copies; a cell does the same.

beats.scene: A round red blood cell with an empty middle beside a normal cell
beats.summary: Almost every cell has a copy of the box, but a mature red blood cell has thrown its box away to make room for oxygen.

beats.scene: Maya writes the first line in her notebook beside a recipe card
beats.summary: Teo gives the cards their scientific name, genes, and Maya writes her first note.

beats.scene: A long twisting ladder of DNA with four coloured letters
beats.summary: Genes are written in DNA, a long molecule with only four letters: A, C, G and T.

beats.scene: Biscuits shaped like the letters A, C, G and T on a tray
beats.summary: Four letters can write endless messages when they are strung together in long chains.

beats.scene: A ladder made of paired coloured blocks, A with T and C with G
beats.summary: The two sides of the ladder are joined by pairs of letters, and A always pairs with T while C always pairs with G.

beats.scene: Two matching sides of a ladder pulled apart like the halves of a zip
beats.summary: Each side of the ladder is a mirror partner of the other, so one side holds the information for both.

beats.scene: An old X-ray photograph shows a cross-shaped pattern of spots
beats.summary: In 1953 the spiral shape of DNA was worked out, helped by X-ray photographs taken by Rosalind Franklin, and it is incredibly thin.

beats.scene: A thin ribbon copy leaves a nucleus carrying the letters of one gene
beats.summary: To use a gene, the cell makes a temporary copy called RNA, which carries the message out while the DNA stays safe.

beats.scene: Three coloured letters are read off a strand like a word
beats.summary: The cell reads the letters three at a time, and each group of three picks one building block.

beats.scene: A table of sixty-four three-letter words matched to twenty coloured beads
beats.summary: Three letters at a time can make sixty-four words, but there are only twenty building blocks, so several words mean the same block.

beats.scene: A strand of coloured beads with a start flag and a stop sign
beats.summary: Reading begins at a start word and ends at a stop word, like the first and last lines of a recipe.

beats.scene: A banana, a bacterium and a girl point at one table of words
beats.summary: The three-letter code is almost the same in every living thing, so a gene from one species can often be read by another.

beats.scene: A folded chain of building blocks forms a small curled machine
beats.summary: The chains fold into proteins, which build the body, carry things and do most of the work.

beats.scene: A long string of beads folds into a tight curled shape like folded pastry
beats.summary: A chain folds into a shape that fits its job, rather as pastry is folded into layers.

beats.scene: A strand of hair and a piece of skin drawn as woven rope
beats.summary: Many proteins are building materials, such as keratin in hair and collagen in skin and bone.

beats.scene: Maya chews a crust of bread while a tiny machine snips starch into sugar
beats.summary: An enzyme in saliva cuts starch into sugar, which is why a chewed crust tastes sweet.

beats.scene: Red blood cells carry bright dots of iron through a thin tube
beats.summary: Haemoglobin makes blood red because it holds iron, which grabs oxygen in the lungs and lets it go where it is needed.

beats.scene: A jar of bubbling sourdough starter beside a rising bowl of dough
beats.summary: Yeast is a tiny living thing with its own genes, and it makes the gas that raises bread.

beats.scene: Round yeast cells budding under a microscope beside a drawing of a human cell
beats.summary: Yeast has about six thousand genes, and some are so old that they do the same job in people.

beats.scene: A worn-out protein is broken apart while a fresh one is built beside it
beats.summary: Proteins wear out, so the cell must read its cards again and again to make new ones.

beats.scene: One recipe card splits into three slightly different dishes
beats.summary: One gene can sometimes make several slightly different proteins, so the body has more kinds of protein than genes.

beats.scene: Maya's notebook page shows three boxes joined by arrows: recipe, copy, worker
beats.summary: Maya sums up the first lesson: DNA holds the recipe, RNA carries a copy, and proteins do the work.

beats.scene: A very long thread of DNA coiled into a tiny nucleus
beats.summary: A human cell holds about three billion DNA letters and about 20,000 genes.

beats.scene: Maya reads a long string of letters aloud while watching the kitchen clock
beats.summary: Reading three billion letters aloud, one every second, would take about a hundred years.

beats.scene: A long thread wound around tiny spools inside a nucleus
beats.summary: DNA is wound around spools made of histone proteins, then coiled and folded to fit inside the nucleus.

beats.scene: Forty-six chromosomes arranged in pairs, half blue and half yellow
beats.summary: DNA is packed into 23 pairs of chromosomes, and you get one of each pair from each parent.

beats.scene: Two chromosomes marked X and Y beside a pair of matching X chromosomes
beats.summary: One pair of chromosomes helps to decide a baby's sex: usually two X chromosomes in a girl, and an X and a Y in a boy.

beats.scene: A long ruler of DNA with only a few small stripes coloured as genes
beats.summary: Only about one or two letters in a hundred belong to protein-making genes, and scientists still disagree about the rest.

beats.scene: A short recipe card and an enormously long one laid side by side
beats.summary: Genes come in very different sizes, from a few hundred letters to more than two million.

beats.scene: A heart cell and a skin cell, each holding the same box
beats.summary: Different cells use different cards, so a heart cell and a skin cell are not the same.

beats.scene: One egg cell divides into two, then four, then eight cells
beats.summary: Every person began as one cell, and as it divided, the cells took on different jobs while keeping the same box.

beats.scene: A bean-shaped power station with its own tiny circle of DNA
beats.summary: Mitochondria are small power stations with a tiny box of their own, which a child normally gets from its mother.

beats.scene: A monk in a garden counts tall and short pea plants
beats.summary: In the 1860s, a monk named Gregor Mendel grew pea plants and found that traits pass on in separate units.

beats.scene: Pea plants with tall and short stems, round and wrinkled seeds
beats.summary: Mendel chose peas because they grow fast, give many seeds, and show clear either-or features.

beats.scene: A monk holds a small brush and moves pollen from one flower to another
beats.summary: Mendel brushed pollen from one plant to another by hand, so he knew exactly which parents each seed had.

beats.scene: A tall pea plant and a short one produce only tall young plants
beats.summary: When Mendel crossed tall plants with short ones, every plant in the next generation was tall.

beats.scene: Young pea plants in a row, three tall stems for every short one
beats.summary: In the next generation the short feature came back in about one plant in four, a ratio of three to one.

beats.scene: A pea plant holds two small cards, one tall and one short
beats.summary: Mendel guessed that each plant holds two units for a feature, one from each parent, and that one can hide the other.

beats.scene: Pots of paint mixing into one colour beside separate cards that stay whole
beats.summary: People thought features blended like paint, but Mendel's units stayed whole and could come back unchanged.

beats.scene: Rows of pea plants in a monastery garden and a notebook full of numbers
beats.summary: Mendel's experiments lasted about eight years and covered many thousands of plants, so his counts were hard to argue with.

beats.scene: An elderly abbot at a desk with a pile of unread papers
beats.summary: Mendel published in 1866 and was almost ignored, and he died in 1884; his work was rediscovered around 1900.

beats.scene: Maya writes Mendel's name beside a row of tally marks in her notebook
beats.summary: Mendel found the rules without ever seeing a gene, and Maya decides to count carefully herself.

beats.scene: Two recipe cards for the same dish, one with more sugar
beats.summary: A gene can come in different versions, and you have two copies of each one.

beats.scene: A round smooth pea beside a shrivelled wrinkled pea on a plate
beats.summary: Wrinkled peas have a faulty version of a gene for building starch, and round peas have a working one.

beats.scene: Two cards in a recipe box, with only the working card being used
beats.summary: When one copy is enough to show a feature, it hides the other version, which can still be passed on.

beats.scene: Two dark-haired parents standing beside a small red-haired child
beats.summary: Red hair usually needs a particular gene version from both parents, so two parents without it can have a red-haired child.

beats.scene: Four boxes drawn in flour on the counter with letters in each
beats.summary: Teo draws a grid in flour to show the four ways that two parents' copies can meet in a child.

beats.scene: Four tubes of blood labelled A, B, AB and O in a rack
beats.summary: A few features, such as the ABO blood group, depend mainly on one gene, but they are the exception.

beats.scene: A crowd of tiny cards combine to decide one person's height
beats.summary: Most traits, such as height, depend on many genes at once, and not on a single gene.

beats.scene: Pencil marks on a pantry doorframe show the family's heights over many years
beats.summary: Maya stands against the doorframe marks and finds that she is near her mother's height at the same age, but not the same.

beats.scene: Twenty small pinches of sugar fall one after another into a mixing bowl
beats.summary: Thousands of small differences add up like pinches in a recipe, so heights form a smooth range with most people in the middle.

beats.scene: A row of eyes in different shades from pale grey to dark brown
beats.summary: Even eye colour depends on several genes, and Maya sums up that cards are handed on whole but their effects combine.

beats.scene: Maya wraps a plaster around her finger beside a baking tin
beats.summary: A small cut heals because nearby cells divide, and each new cell needs its own full copy of the DNA.

beats.scene: A tall stack of thick novels beside a single tiny cell
beats.summary: Copying three billion letters is like copying thousands of novels by hand, and it must be done accurately each time.

beats.scene: DNA splits like a zip, and each half builds a new matching half
beats.summary: Before a cell divides, its DNA is copied, and the copying is very careful.

beats.scene: Many small copying machines work along one strand of DNA at the same time
beats.summary: A cell starts copying at thousands of places at once, so the job is done in hours instead of taking far too long.

beats.scene: A small machine slides along an opened strand, adding matching letters
beats.summary: A copying protein called DNA polymerase adds the matching letter opposite each letter, building a new partner side.

beats.scene: A magnifying glass above a copied strand, with one wrong letter being cut out
beats.summary: The copying machine checks each new letter as it goes, and backs up to fix any wrong one.

beats.scene: Tiny repair workers with lamps inspect a finished strand of DNA
beats.summary: Repair proteins check the new strand for mismatched pairs, and only about one letter in a billion is left wrong.

beats.scene: Red blood cells pour out of a bone beside a patch of skin
beats.summary: The body makes about two million red blood cells every second, and skin renews itself about monthly, all by copying DNA.

beats.scene: A long branching nerve cell rests among small round skin cells
beats.summary: Not every cell keeps dividing: most nerve cells stop early in life, while skin and blood cells are replaced constantly.

beats.scene: Teo points to a single smudged letter on a long page of tiny writing
beats.summary: Even a tiny error rate adds up over three billion letters and trillions of cells, so some mistakes always slip through.

beats.scene: One tiny letter on a copied strand is wrong, glowing red
beats.summary: Sometimes a mistake slips through, and a changed letter is called a mutation.

beats.scene: One card reads THE CAT SAW THE DOG, another reads THE CAR SAW
beats.summary: Swapping one letter changes only one three-letter word, so the damage is small.

beats.scene: A card with an extra letter and every later word scrambled
beats.summary: If a letter is added or lost, every three-letter word after it changes, so the whole message can be ruined.

beats.scene: A recipe with one smudged word that makes no difference to the cake
beats.summary: Most mutations do nothing, a few do harm, and a very few help.

beats.scene: Two different three-letter words point to the same coloured bead
beats.summary: Because several words mean the same building block, many swaps are silent and change nothing.

beats.scene: A cake with a wrong ingredient and a baker looking worried
beats.summary: A few mutations change the protein so much that it works badly or not at all, and some cause illness.

beats.scene: Pale mice on white beach sand and dark mice on dark soil
beats.summary: A very few mutations help, and it depends on the place: pale beach mice in Florida are harder for owls to see on pale sand.

beats.scene: Sunlight falls on a hand while a tiny cut appears in DNA
beats.summary: Most mutations are copying mistakes, but ultraviolet light and some chemicals can also damage DNA, and cells repair most of it.

beats.scene: A skin cell fades away while an egg cell passes on a glowing letter
beats.summary: A mutation in an ordinary body cell stays in that body; only changes in egg or sperm cells can be passed on to children.

beats.scene: Rows of different recipe cards, each tracing back to one smudged original
beats.summary: Every version of every gene began as a one-time mistake, and without mutations all the cards would be alike.

beats.scene: A box of cards in slightly different handwriting for each family member
beats.summary: After many copies, the cards differ a little, so no two individuals have exactly the same recipes.

beats.scene: Three handwritten copies of one cake card, each with a small change
beats.summary: Carmen's copy of the family cake card has drifted from Rosa's, and the versions that tasted best were copied again.

beats.scene: Fast and slow rabbits in a field, a fox chasing the slower ones
beats.summary: Some versions help an animal survive and raise young, and so they get copied more often.

beats.scene: A cod surrounded by thousands of tiny eggs beside an oak dropping acorns
beats.summary: A cod lays millions of eggs and an oak drops thousands of acorns, but almost none of them survive.

beats.scene: Two finches on a dry island, one with a thick beak, one slender
beats.summary: In a drought on a Galapagos island, finches with deeper beaks survived better, and their chicks had deeper beaks.

beats.scene: A dish with a few surviving bacteria after medicine is added
beats.summary: Bacteria change quickly, so a few that resist a medicine can survive and multiply fast.

beats.scene: A dish with a clear ring around a patch of mould
beats.summary: In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed that a mould had killed bacteria around it, which led to the medicine penicillin.

beats.scene: A doctor hands a small box of medicine to a patient
beats.summary: Each use of an antibiotic gives resistant bacteria a better chance, so doctors ask people to use these medicines only when needed.

beats.scene: A flour sieve lets fine grains fall through while larger lumps stay behind
beats.summary: Natural selection has no planner; like a sieve, it keeps what works and lets the rest fall away.

beats.scene: Maya's notebook page listing survivors, beside a rabbit and a loaf
beats.summary: The cards in living things today are the survivors of a very long process of copying.

beats.scene: Recipe cards from long ago are copied again and again through the years
beats.summary: The copies that last are the ones that helped earlier bodies to survive, so useful genes spread.

beats.scene: A long line of hands passes one worn recipe card down the generations
beats.summary: Useful means good at getting copied: every card in the box today belongs to a long line of successes.

beats.scene: A pea plant and a cow stand under one banner of nearly identical proteins
beats.summary: One histone protein is almost the same in peas and cattle, differing in only two places, although plants and animals parted over a billion years ago.

beats.scene: Maya shakes her head as a recipe card has a thought bubble crossed out
beats.summary: Genes do not think or want anything, and the word wants is only a way to describe what happens.

beats.scene: Rosa smiles at a stack of favourite recipe cards worn soft at the edges
beats.summary: Rosa says her recipes never wanted to be baked, but the best-loved ones were baked again, and that is all that is meant.

beats.scene: An old stone bridge stands beside a heap of fallen bricks
beats.summary: We see old things because they were built to last; the old genes we see are the ones that kept being copied.

beats.scene: A parent animal carries a glowing copy of a gene inside its body
beats.summary: A gene travels inside a body, so it is tested by how well that body survives and has young.

beats.scene: A diagram of an eye with nerve fibres lying in front of the sensors
beats.summary: Evolution only changes what already exists, so the human eye has a blind spot where nerves pass through, while the octopus eye has none.

beats.scene: A very long strip of paper marked with the age of the Earth
beats.summary: The Earth is about four and a half billion years old and life is more than three billion years old, so there has been a very long time for changes to add up.

beats.scene: Maya reads her notebook aloud to Rosa with flour on her hands
beats.summary: At midsummer Maya reads her notebook to Rosa, who says her own mother would have loved it.

beats.scene: Tiny fruit flies hover above a bowl of overripe bananas on the counter
beats.summary: Fruit flies appear in the bakery, and Teo says that these tiny insects taught scientists a great deal about genes.

beats.scene: A fruit fly and a person side by side, sharing old genes
beats.summary: Hox genes, which plan the body, are found in flies and in people, and they are very old.

beats.scene: A fly with legs growing from its head where its antennae should be
beats.summary: A changed Hox gene can make a fly grow legs where its antennae should be, showing that Hox genes tell cells what to build.

beats.scene: A recipe card photocopied twice, with one copy slightly changed
beats.summary: A cell sometimes copies a whole gene by accident, and the spare is free to change and do a new job.

beats.scene: A strand of human DNA with a short piece drawn as a tiny virus
beats.summary: About eight in every hundred letters of our DNA came from ancient viruses.

beats.scene: A virus pushes a ribbon of its own letters into a cell's DNA
beats.summary: Retroviruses paste a copy of their instructions into a cell's DNA, and if that happens in an egg or sperm, a child can inherit it.

beats.scene: Small pieces of DNA hop from place to place along a long strand
beats.summary: Jumping genes copy themselves into new places, and their old remains make up close to half of human DNA.

beats.scene: Corn kernels speckled with spots of many colours on a single cob
beats.summary: In the 1940s Barbara McClintock explained speckled maize kernels by jumping genes, and she won a Nobel Prize in 1983.

beats.scene: A Neanderthal skull beside a modern human skull and a strand of DNA
beats.summary: People with ancestors from outside Africa carry about one or two letters in every hundred from Neanderthals, who had children with early modern humans.

beats.scene: A scientist in a clean white suit holds an ancient bone in a laboratory
beats.summary: Scientists can read DNA from bones tens of thousands of years old, so the box is also a history book.

beats.scene: Two red blood cells, one round and one bent like a sickle
beats.summary: One version of a haemoglobin gene protects against malaria in one copy, but causes illness in two.

beats.scene: A round red blood cell beside a bent sickle-shaped cell
beats.summary: In sickle cell disease one changed letter swaps a building block, and the faulty haemoglobin bends the cells.

beats.scene: A mosquito lands on the arm of a sleeping child
beats.summary: Malaria is a serious illness spread by mosquitoes, caused by a tiny parasite that lives in red blood cells.

beats.scene: A world map with the sickle version marked in Africa, the Mediterranean and India
beats.summary: The sickle version is most common where malaria was common, so the pattern follows the illness and not any group of people.

beats.scene: Maya sits with her notebook beside a drawing of two red blood cells
beats.summary: The same gene version can protect in one way and harm in another, and nature has no plan to be fair.

beats.scene: A herder with cows and a child drinking a cup of milk
beats.summary: In people whose ancestors kept cattle, many adults can still digest milk, thanks to a gene change.

beats.scene: Two cattle herders, one in Africa and one in Europe, with different glowing letters
beats.summary: Herding peoples in Europe and East Africa each evolved milk-digesting adults, through different changes near the lactase gene.

beats.scene: A cheese board and a bowl of yoghurt beside a jug of milk
beats.summary: Cheese and yoghurt hold less lactose than fresh milk, because microbes use some of it up.

beats.scene: Climbers in a thin-aired high valley with snowy peaks
beats.summary: Many people in Tibet carry a version of a gene called EPAS1 that helps the body cope with thin air.

beats.scene: Three mountain peoples, each beside a different gene card
beats.summary: People in the Andes and Ethiopia cope with thin air using other genes, and the Tibetan EPAS1 version may have come from the Denisovans.

beats.scene: Several recipe cards used together to make one layered cake
beats.summary: No gene works alone, because each one works with many others in the same body.

beats.scene: A chain of recipe cards, each one pointing with an arrow to the next
beats.summary: Many genes switch other genes on and off, so the cards form chains and networks that can build a heart or a leaf.

beats.scene: Two decks of cards are shuffled together into a new deck
beats.summary: Before an egg or sperm is made, the cards are shuffled, so each child gets a new mix.

beats.scene: Egg and sperm cells each carry one chromosome from every pair, then join
beats.summary: A special division called meiosis makes egg and sperm cells with half the chromosomes, and joining restores twenty-three pairs.

beats.scene: Maya flips twenty-three coins on the counter, each showing one of two faces
beats.summary: Each parent can make over eight million different combinations of chromosomes by chance alone, before any pieces are swapped.

beats.scene: Teo holds an old photograph of himself and his sister Elena as children
beats.summary: Teo and his sister Elena, Maya's mother, had the same parents but look quite different, because each was dealt a different hand.

beats.scene: Different workers with different tools fit together around one table
beats.summary: Because the cards are shuffled, a gene version keeps meeting new partners, so the versions that last work well with many partners.

beats.scene: Cards from two boxes laid out in many combinations on a table
beats.summary: Scientists have several ideas about why sex exists, and none of them explains everything.

beats.scene: A jar of sourdough starter buds into new yeast cells beside a dandelion
beats.summary: Many living things copy themselves without sex: yeast bud and many dandelions make seeds with no partner, so the young are near clones.

beats.scene: A deck of cards is shuffled and dealt into two hands
beats.summary: Each child is a new hand dealt from two old decks, and the particular hand has never been dealt before.

beats.scene: A wall of framed family photographs above the bakery counter
beats.summary: Maya spots her grandmother's nose on her own face and asks why families look alike.

beats.scene: A grandmother, a mother and a child with matching recipe cards
beats.summary: You share about half your gene versions with a parent, child or sibling, and less with cousins.

beats.scene: Two nearly identical strands of DNA with a few coloured differences
beats.summary: The half refers to the small number of places where people differ, because everyone shares almost all of their DNA.

beats.scene: A family tree drawn on a paper bag with a fraction beside each person
beats.summary: Maya works out her own shares: one half with her mother Elena, and one quarter each with her grandmother Rosa and her uncle Teo.

beats.scene: Two identical babies and two non-identical babies lying side by side
beats.summary: Identical twins come from one egg that splits and share almost all their DNA, while non-identical twins share about half, like other siblings.

beats.scene: A young scientist in 1964 sketches a family tree on a sheet of paper
beats.summary: In 1964 William Hamilton explained that a gene which makes animals help relatives can spread, because relatives carry copies of it.

beats.scene: Scales with a cost on one side and a benefit on the other
beats.summary: Helping tends to spread when the benefit to a relative, reduced by how distant that relative is, outweighs the cost to the helper.

beats.scene: Rosa wraps a fresh loaf in paper for her sister Carmen with a smile
beats.summary: Rosa gives bread to her sister out of love, and the sum describes why such feelings could spread, not what people feel.

beats.scene: A ground squirrel stands up in a meadow and calls as others hide
beats.summary: Researchers found that female ground squirrels with relatives nearby gave alarm calls more often than females with none.

beats.scene: Maya looks from the photograph wall out of the window at the busy street
beats.summary: Relatedness is not the whole story, because people and animals also help friends and strangers.

beats.scene: A mother bird feeds wide-open beaks in a nest
beats.summary: Parents care for young, and the young carry copies of half of their parents' genes.

beats.scene: Blue tits carry caterpillars to a nest box full of open beaks
beats.summary: Parent tits may make hundreds of trips a day, and feeding a big family is so tiring that parents must save strength for the future.

beats.scene: Worker bees tend a larger queen bee inside a honeycomb
beats.summary: Worker bees do not have young, but they help their mother the queen, who passes on copies of shared genes.

beats.scene: Dario in a beekeeper's veil shows Maya a frame of honeycomb
beats.summary: In honeybees, males hatch from unfertilised eggs, so sisters with the same father share about three quarters of their gene versions.

beats.scene: A queen bee on a mating flight with several drones above a hill
beats.summary: A honeybee queen mates with about a dozen drones, so most workers are half sisters, and scientists argue about how much the arithmetic explains.

beats.scene: Bats hang in a row in a cave, one feeding another
beats.summary: Vampire bats share food with roost mates who shared with them, as well as with relatives.

beats.scene: A vampire bat feeds a hungry roost mate in a dark cave
beats.summary: A vampire bat that misses two or three nights of feeding may starve, so sharing a blood meal can save a life.

beats.scene: A bat turns away from a hungry neighbour who has never shared
beats.summary: Trading favours works when the same animals meet again and cheats can be refused.

beats.scene: A baby animal tugging at its mother who turns away
beats.summary: Young animals often want more milk than their mothers are ready to give, so families can disagree.

beats.scene: Maya holds a telephone to her ear in the kitchen on a Sunday
beats.summary: Maya phones her mother and decides that a family is both a team and a quarrel, though mostly a team.

beats.scene: A small bird feeds a giant cuckoo chick that fills the whole nest
beats.summary: A cuckoo chick tricks other birds into feeding it, and some hosts have learned to spot the trick.

beats.scene: A cuckoo lands on a reed warbler's nest and slips an egg inside
beats.summary: A female cuckoo lays her egg in a few seconds while the host is away, and her chick hatches a little earlier than the host's own.

beats.scene: A row of speckled eggs, with one cuckoo egg hard to tell apart
beats.summary: Cuckoo eggs often look like the host's eggs, because hosts that spot a poor copy throw it out.

beats.scene: A cuckoo chick with its beak wide open among small host chicks
beats.summary: A cuckoo chick begs with rapid calls that sound like a whole brood, so its foster parents keep bringing food.

beats.scene: A frog fights a growing line of tiny parasites on a leaf
beats.summary: Hosts and parasites keep changing to beat each other, and neither stays ahead for long.

beats.scene: Alice and the Red Queen run hand in hand across a chessboard landscape
beats.summary: Biologists call this contest the Red Queen effect, after a character in Through the Looking-Glass who says you must run to stay in place.

beats.scene: Pond snails with tiny parasites in a lake in New Zealand
beats.summary: In lakes where parasites were common, more of a small snail's population reproduced with partners, which fits the idea that sex helps against parasites.

beats.scene: An ant clings to a leaf with a thin stalk growing from its head
beats.summary: A fungus can take over a carpenter ant's behaviour, making it climb a plant and bite on, though scientists are still learning how.

beats.scene: A white blood cell inspects a tiny germ with a magnifying glass
beats.summary: The immune system is in an arms race too: some of the most varied human genes help to recognise germs, and flu viruses change every year.

beats.scene: Maya writes in her notebook beside a loaf with a spot of mould
beats.summary: In nature nobody wins for good, because every new defence meets a new attack.

beats.scene: A puppeteer's strings are cut and a puppet stands on its own legs
beats.summary: Genes are not puppet strings, because they only shape how a brain and body develop.

beats.scene: Two identical boys in matching coats choose different buns at the counter
beats.summary: Ines, a nurse, buys bread each morning with her identical twin sons Leo and Nico, who look the same but choose different buns.

beats.scene: Two identical twin girls with different hairstyles and hobbies
beats.summary: Identical twins share nearly all their DNA, yet they still differ in many ways.

beats.scene: Two seedlings from one packet grow differently in two different spots
beats.summary: Identical twins differ because of a few tiny mutations, chance during growth, the womb and different experiences.

beats.scene: Tiny pencil notes in the margin of a recipe card
beats.summary: Chemical tags on DNA can turn genes up or down, and the tags of identical twins drift apart with age.

beats.scene: A chart of people of different heights beside a table of food
beats.summary: When scientists say a trait is half inherited, they mean something about differences in a group.

beats.scene: Two lines of people, the grandchildren standing taller than the great-grandparents
beats.summary: In many countries, average height has risen by several centimetres in a hundred years because of better food and health, while genes changed little.

beats.scene: A shelf of thousands of tiny dials, each turned a little
beats.summary: There is no single gene for being a baker or for being kind; behaviour comes from thousands of nudges and from life, and a nudge is not a destiny.

beats.scene: A baby having a small heel-prick test in a hospital room
beats.summary: A gene version can cause harm in one world and be harmless in another, as with phenylketonuria.

beats.scene: Maya shapes dough into rolls with her own hands while Rosa watches
beats.summary: Maya says that her genes helped to give her her hands, but she is the one learning what to do with them.

beats.scene: A crowd of people of all kinds seen from above, linked by faint lines
beats.summary: Any two people share almost all of their DNA, and most differences are found within groups.

beats.scene: A short timeline of human history beside a very long timeline of life
beats.summary: Our species is young, about three hundred thousand years old, so there has been little time for large differences to build up.

beats.scene: A world map with arrows leaving Africa and spreading to other continents
beats.summary: Our species began in Africa, and the groups that left about sixty thousand years ago took only part of its variety, so Africa holds more variety than any other region.

beats.scene: Hands of different shades beside a long strand of DNA with few stripes
beats.summary: The features people notice first, such as skin colour, depend largely on a few genes out of about twenty thousand, and they say little about the rest of a person.

beats.scene: A person, a chimpanzee, a mouse and a fruit fly in a family portrait
beats.summary: Humans share more than 98 out of 100 DNA letters with chimpanzees, and many genes with mice and flies.

beats.scene: A branching tree in flour, ending in a girl, ape, mouse, fly and yeast
beats.summary: The more recently two branches split, the more alike their DNA tends to be; humans and chimpanzees split about six or seven million years ago.

beats.scene: A tiny worm, a person and a rice plant beside piles of cards
beats.summary: A tiny worm has about as many genes as a person, and rice has more, so the number of genes does not decide how complicated a living thing is.

beats.scene: Mice and flies in a clean laboratory beside a person in a white coat
beats.summary: Scientists switch off a gene in a fly, a worm or a mouse to learn what it does, then look for the human version in people with a related problem.

beats.scene: Two bacteria pass a tiny loop of DNA between them
beats.summary: Bacteria pass small loops of DNA called plasmids to each other, even between species, so a gene for resisting a medicine can spread sideways.

beats.scene: Maya writes the word cousin beside every tip of the tree drawn in flour
beats.summary: Maya writes cousin beside every tip of the tree, seeing that everything alive belongs to one very big family.

beats.scene: A wolf at one end and several different dogs at the other
beats.summary: People have changed the genes of other species by choosing which ones to breed, as with dogs.

beats.scene: A silver fox with floppy ears wags its tail beside a researcher's hand
beats.summary: In Siberia from 1959, scientists bred only the tamest foxes, and within about ten generations some were friendly, with floppy ears and spotted coats.

beats.scene: A wild plant on a seaside cliff beside cabbage, kale, broccoli and cauliflower
beats.summary: Cabbage, kale, broccoli and cauliflower all came from one wild plant, shaped by farmers who kept the parts they liked.

beats.scene: Tall maize plants beside a small wild grass with a few seeds
beats.summary: Crops such as maize were shaped by farmers choosing seeds from the best plants over many years.

beats.scene: A field of golden wheat beside a loaf of bread on Rosa's counter
beats.summary: Bread wheat has a genome about five times larger than ours and forty-two chromosomes, because three wild grasses combined their sets.

beats.scene: A scientist's glove holds a tiny pair of scissors beside a DNA strand
beats.summary: In 2012, a tool called CRISPR made editing genes much easier, and one treatment was approved in 2023.

beats.scene: Tiny scissors, guided by a short strand, find a matching spot on DNA
beats.summary: CRISPR began as a bacterial defence against viruses; scientists use a short guide strand to lead a cutting protein to a chosen place in DNA.

beats.scene: A doctor and a patient look at a small bag of edited blood-making cells
beats.summary: The sickle cell treatment edits a patient's own blood-making cells so that they make the haemoglobin that babies use, which does not bend into sickle shapes.

beats.scene: People around a table discuss papers and a drawing of a DNA strand
beats.summary: Editing one patient's cells affects only that person, but edits in eggs, sperm or embryos would be inherited, so many countries limit them.

beats.scene: A thin machine reads a strand of DNA while a screen shows letters
beats.summary: Reading a whole genome once took many years and billions of dollars, and now it is much faster and cheaper.

beats.scene: A doctor and a patient look at a page of gene results together
beats.summary: A gene test usually shows chances, not certainties, and a doctor can help to understand it.

beats.scene: A page of gene results laid beside a family tree
beats.summary: Relatives share gene versions, so one person's test also says something about their family, which makes privacy important.

beats.scene: A lion catches a gazelle while a person offers a hand to a neighbour
beats.summary: Natural does not mean good, and what evolution has produced does not tell us how we should live.

beats.scene: Rosa puts on her glasses to read a faded recipe card while Teo smiles
beats.summary: Glasses, vaccines and medicines all go against what nature would do alone, so the question that matters is whether something is kind, fair and wise.

beats.scene: A teacher, a book, a song and a child, all connected by lines
beats.summary: People also pass on ideas, skills and customs, so we are more than our genes.

beats.scene: A humpback whale sings under the waves while a bird sings on a branch
beats.summary: Animals pass on what they learn too: humpback whales spread new songs across the Pacific, and young birds learn songs from adults.

beats.scene: A long line of parents and children going back to one cell
beats.summary: Every gene in you was copied through an unbroken line of ancestors back to the first cells.

beats.scene: A family tree that doubles in every row while some branches join together again
beats.summary: On paper you have over a billion ancestors thirty generations back, which is more than were alive, so the same people appear many times.

beats.scene: Lanterns, neighbours and tables of bread fill the bakery at a party
beats.summary: At Rosa's party, Maya answers Teo's last question: a gene is a recipe that is copied and tested in a body, and it never wants anything.

beats.summary: Maya adds a new card to the box, and Teo says she is a new edition of an old book.

B1B2: Maya has found an old wooden box of recipe cards in her grandmother Rosa's bakery. Her uncle Teo says that every living thing carries a box like it.
Rosa wiped her floury hands and said that the box had belonged to her own mother. Every card in it had been copied out by hand, and some of the cards were older than she was.
Maya asked what he meant, and Teo laughed and said the answer would take all summer. He offered a deal: she could ask one question every day while they worked, and he would answer it honestly.
A recipe card does not bake anything by itself, because it only tells a baker what to do. A gene is the same, because it is a set of instructions for making one useful part of a living thing.

Rosa's card for plain bread lists only four ingredients, which are flour, water, salt and yeast. The steps matter as much as the list, because the same four things in the wrong order do not make bread.
Rosa baked two loaves from the same card on two different days, and they did not look quite alike. The oven was hotter on one day, and the air was damper on the other.
Your body is made of trillions of tiny rooms called cells, and each one works like a kitchen. Almost every cell keeps its own complete copy of the recipe box inside a part called the nucleus.
Rosa never carries the old cards into the messy kitchen, because flour and butter would ruin them. Instead she copies a card and lets the bakers work from the copy.
Maya asked whether every single cell has the box, and Teo said almost every one does. A mature red blood cell throws its box away, which leaves more room for carrying oxygen.
Teo told Maya that the scientific name for a card is a gene. She opened her notebook and wrote that a gene is a recipe for one useful thing.
The recipes are written in a long, twisted molecule called DNA. It uses only four letters, which are A, C, G and T, and the order of the letters is what matters.

Rosa baked biscuits in the shapes of A, C, G and T, and Teo lined them up on the tray. He explained that four letters are enough to write endless messages, as long as they are strung together in long chains.
The two sides of the DNA ladder are joined by rungs, and each rung is a pair of letters. The pairing never changes: A always sits opposite T, and C always sits opposite G.
Because of the pairing rule, each side of the ladder is a perfect partner of the other. If you know the letters on one side, you can always work out the letters on the other.

The spiral shape of DNA was worked out in 1953, and X-ray photographs taken by Rosalind Franklin gave an important clue. The ladder is only about two billionths of a metre wide, tens of thousands of times thinner than a hair.
When the cell needs a gene, it makes a temporary copy of that gene on a thin strand called RNA. The copy travels out to the cooks, while the precious DNA stays safely inside.
The cell reads DNA three letters at a time, like words in a sentence. Each group of three tells it which building block to add next.

Four letters taken three at a time can make sixty-four different words, but the cell needs only twenty building blocks. So several different words can point to the same block, which is a little like having two names for one thing.
Reading does not begin just anywhere, because a special start word tells the cell where a gene begins. A stop word at the end tells it that the chain is finished.
The code is almost exactly the same in bananas, bacteria and people. This means that a gene from one living thing can often be read by another.
The finished chain folds up into a protein, and proteins do most of the work in the body. Some build hair, some digest food, and one called haemoglobin carries oxygen in your blood.
A new chain does not stay straight, because it folds itself into a very particular shape. The shape decides the job, in the same way that a key's shape decides which lock it opens.
Many proteins are building materials, like the bricks and beams of a house. Keratin makes hair and nails, and collagen is a strong, rope-like protein that gives strength to skin, bones and tendons.
Some proteins are tiny machines called enzymes, and each one does a single job very fast. One in your saliva cuts the starch in bread into sugar, so a chewed crust slowly tastes sweet.
Haemoglobin is the protein that makes blood red, because each molecule holds some iron. The iron catches oxygen in the lungs and releases it where the body needs it.
Yeast is a tiny living thing with its own recipe box, and the box has genes for eating sugar. As the yeast feeds, it makes a gas that fills the dough with bubbles.
A yeast cell has about six thousand genes, which is far fewer than a person has. Even so, some of its genes are so old that they do the same jobs in human cells.
Proteins do not last forever, because they wear out and are broken up for parts. A cell therefore goes back to its cards again and again to make fresh ones.
A cell can sometimes read one gene in more than one way and make slightly different proteins. This is one reason why people have more kinds of protein than they have genes.
At the end of the week, Maya wrote a summary in her notebook. DNA holds the recipes, RNA carries a copy, and proteins do the work.
A human cell holds about three billion DNA letters and about 20,000 genes. If you stretched out the DNA from one cell, it would be about two metres long.
Teo asked Maya to imagine reading the three billion letters aloud, one every second, without a break. It would take her about a hundred years, and that is only the letters in one set.
The long thread of DNA is wound around tiny spools made of proteins called histones. The spools are then coiled and folded again and again, like a thread packed into a sewing box.
DNA is packed into bundles called chromosomes, and a human cell has 23 pairs of them. You received one chromosome of each pair from your mother and the other from your father.
Twenty-two of the pairs are numbered, and the twenty-third pair is special because it helps to decide a baby's sex. Usually a girl has two X chromosomes, while a boy has one X and one much smaller Y.
Only about one or two letters in every hundred belong to genes that make proteins. Some of the rest has other jobs, some may do nothing, and scientists disagree about how much is which.
Genes come in very different sizes, from a few hundred letters up to more than two million. The longest human gene is like a recipe card that stretches right across the kitchen.
Your heart cells and your skin cells hold the same recipe box, but they use different cards. Part of the DNA acts as a set of switches that decide which genes are turned on.

Each person began as one single cell, which divided into two, then four, then eight. Every new cell kept the same recipe box, but as they multiplied they began to use different cards for different jobs.
Every cell also holds small power stations called mitochondria, and each one has a tiny recipe box of its own. A child normally receives all of its mitochondria from its mother, not from its father.

In the 1860s, a monk named Gregor Mendel grew thousands of pea plants and counted their tall and short offspring. He saw that traits are passed on in separate units, although nobody yet knew what those units were.
Mendel chose peas because they grow quickly in a garden and produce many seeds. Their features also come in clear pairs, such as tall or short stems and round or wrinkled seeds.
Mendel moved pollen from one flower to another with a small brush. This way he knew exactly which two plants were the parents of every seed.
When Mendel crossed a tall plant with a short one, all of the new plants were tall. The short feature seemed to have vanished completely, and he wondered where it had gone.
Next he let the tall plants of the new generation pollinate themselves. The short feature returned in about one plant in four, so there were roughly three tall plants for every short one.
Mendel guessed that each plant holds two units for every feature, one from each parent. A unit can be hidden by its partner and then appear again in the next generation.

People then thought that parents' features blended like paint, so that children were always a mixture. Mendel's peas showed something different, because the units stayed whole and could come back unchanged.
Mendel did not give up quickly, because he grew and counted plants for about eight years. In the end he had records of many thousands of plants, which made his numbers very hard to argue with.
Mendel published his results in 1866 in a local journal, but hardly anyone took notice. He became the head of his monastery, and he died in 1884 without knowing how important his work would be.

Maya wrote in her notebook that Mendel had found the rules without ever seeing a gene. Teo smiled and said that careful counting can reveal a pattern long before anyone understands the machinery behind it.

Most genes come in slightly different versions, rather like two cards for the same cake that call for different amounts of sugar. Because you have two copies of each gene, you may hold two different versions.

In Mendel's wrinkled peas, one version of a gene is faulty, and it cannot make a protein that builds starch. The seeds hold too much sugar and too little starch, so they shrink and wrinkle as they dry.
When one copy of a gene is enough to show a feature, scientists call that version dominant. The other version, called recessive, can stay hidden for generations and still be handed on.
Red hair usually appears only when a child receives a particular version of one gene from both parents. The parents may not have red hair themselves, but each one can carry a hidden copy.
Teo drew four boxes in the flour, with one parent's copies along the top and the other's down the side. Each box showed one way that the two copies could meet in a child.
A few features follow Mendel's rules neatly, and the ABO blood group is one of them. It depends mainly on a single gene with three common versions, called A, B and O.
Many people talk about a gene for height or for a talent, but that is a simplification. Most traits are shaped by thousands of small effects added together, and by the world around us.
In the pantry, pencil marks on the doorframe showed how tall each child in the family had been at twelve. Maya stood against it and found that she was close to her mother's mark, but not the same.
Think of height as a recipe made of thousands of small pinches and spoonfuls. Each pinch adds or takes away a tiny amount, so heights form a smooth range, with most people near the middle.

Even eye colour, which looks so simple, is shaped by several genes, with one or two doing most of the work. Maya wrote in her notebook that cards are handed on whole, but their effects can combine in many ways.

Maya cut her finger on the edge of a baking tin, and by the next week the cut had almost gone. Teo said that nearby cells had divided to fill the gap, and each new cell needed its own copy of the box.
Copying three billion letters is like copying out thousands of novels by hand. A single cell must do that job, with very few mistakes, every time it divides.
Before a cell divides, it unzips its DNA and builds a new partner for each half. Special proteins check the work as they go, so mistakes are very rare.
One machine copying from one end to the other would take far too long. So the cell starts the job at thousands of places at once, and many small machines work along the thread together.
The main copying machine is a protein with a long name, which is DNA polymerase. It slides along one side of the opened ladder and adds the matching letter for every letter that it meets.
The copying machine checks every new letter as soon as it is added. If a wrong letter has slipped in, the machine backs up, cuts it out and tries again.
When the copying is finished, a second team of proteins checks the new strand for pairs that do not match. After all this care, only about one letter in a billion is wrong, or even fewer.
Your body makes about two million new red blood cells every second, and your skin renews itself every month or so. Behind all of it, cells are copying their DNA again and again.
Not every cell in the body keeps on copying itself and dividing. Most nerve cells stop dividing early in life and last for many years, while skin and blood cells are replaced constantly.

One mistake in a billion letters sounds perfect, but a cell has billions of letters and the body has trillions of cells. Teo said that some mistakes will always slip through, and the next lesson was about what happens to them.
Now and then the copying goes wrong, and one letter changes. A change in the DNA is called a mutation, and every person is born with a few dozen new ones.
Teo wrote a sentence of three-letter words on a card: THE CAT SAW THE DOG. When he swapped one letter, it became THE CAR SAW THE DOG, and only one word was changed.
Then Teo added one extra letter near the start, and the sentence became THE ZCA TSA WTH EDO G. Every word after the mistake was broken, because the cell reads in groups of three.
Most mutations make no difference, as when a smudged word on a card does not change the cake. A few do harm, a very few help, and none of them are made because they are needed.
Because several words can mean the same building block, many swaps are silent. A change in the third letter of a word, for example, often leaves the protein exactly as it was.
Some mutations change an important building block, and then the protein cannot do its job properly. A few of these changes cause illnesses, and some can be passed on in families.
In Florida, some mice live on pale beach sand, and they carry a mutation that makes their fur light. On pale sand, hunting owls find them harder to see, so the change helps.

Most mutations come from copying mistakes, but DNA can also be damaged from outside. Ultraviolet rays in strong sunlight and chemicals in tobacco smoke are two examples, and cells repair most of the damage.
A mutation in a skin or muscle cell stays in that one body and ends when the person dies. Only a change in an egg or a sperm cell can be handed on to a child.
Maya realised that every different version of a gene must once have begun as a mistake. Without mutations, every living thing would have exactly the same cards, and nothing could ever change.
Because mutations keep appearing, the cards in a population slowly drift apart. Every group of living things therefore contains many small differences.

Rosa's sister Carmen keeps her own copy of the family cake card, and it is not quite the same as Rosa's. Each time the card was copied, someone changed a little, and the versions that tasted best were copied again.
More young are born than can survive, so some do better than others. The ones that live and have young pass on their gene versions, and that is natural selection.
A cod can lay millions of eggs in a single year, and an old oak tree can drop thousands of acorns. If they all grew up, the world would soon be full of cod and oaks, but almost none do.
On a Galapagos island, a long drought left mostly hard, tough seeds. Finches with deeper beaks could crack them, so more of those finches survived, and their chicks also had deeper beaks.
Bacteria can divide in about twenty minutes, so change comes quickly. If a few of them resist an antibiotic, they survive, and soon the whole group is resistant.

In 1928, a scientist named Alexander Fleming noticed a clear ring around a patch of mould on a dish of bacteria. The mould was making a substance that killed them, and it led to the medicine penicillin.
Each time an antibiotic is used, any resistant bacteria have a better chance to spread. That is why doctors ask people to use these medicines only when really needed, and to follow their advice.
Natural selection does not plan anything, and there is nobody behind it who is choosing. It works like a sieve, which keeps the versions that happen to work and lets the others fall away.
Maya wrote in her notebook that the cards in living things today are the survivors. Teo nodded and said that she had just understood one of the biggest ideas in biology.
What lasts through time is not a body but the instructions that build it. A useful version of a gene can be copied through thousands of bodies and many thousands of years.
When biologists say a gene version is useful, they mean it helps its bodies to survive and have young. A gene succeeds when copies of it reach the next generation, and nothing more.
One of the histone proteins that wrap DNA is almost the same in a pea plant and a cow. It differs in only two places, even though plants and animals went their separate ways over a billion years ago.
Teo reminded Maya that genes do not think, plan or want anything. Saying that a gene wants to be copied is only a short way to describe what happens.
Rosa said that she had never thought of a recipe wanting to be baked. Still, the cards that people loved were baked again and again, while the unloved ones sank to the bottom of the box.
Look at the oldest bridges in a town, and you will see only the strongest ones. The weak bridges fell down long ago, so what remains is not a fair sample of everything that was built.
A gene cannot copy itself into the next generation unless the body that carries it survives and has young. So every gene is tested by how well the body it helps to build gets on in the world.
Evolution never starts again from nothing, so it can only improve what already exists. The human eye has a blind spot where the nerves leave the back of the eye, but an octopus eye has none.
The Earth is about four and a half billion years old, and life has existed for at least three billion of them. That is plenty of time for very tiny changes to add up to something large.

Halfway through the summer, Maya read her whole notebook aloud to Rosa one evening. It told of recipes, workers, copying, mistakes and survivors, and Rosa said that her own mother would have loved to hear it.
In July, tiny fruit flies appeared above a bowl of overripe bananas, and Rosa waved her cloth at them. Teo stopped her and said that those little flies had taught scientists a great deal about genes.
Some genes are very old, and they are shared by many animals. A family called the Hox genes helps to plan which body parts grow where, and flies and humans both have them.
In one strange fly, a changed Hox gene made legs grow on the head, where the feelers should have been. The gene did not build the legs itself, but told the head cells to build them.
Sometimes a whole gene is copied by mistake, and a body ends up with two copies. One copy keeps doing the old job, while the spare is free to change and do something new.
Some of our DNA has a surprising origin, because it did not come from our parents. About eight in every hundred letters came from viruses that infected our ancestors long ago.

A virus is a tiny package of instructions that tricks a cell into making more viruses. Some kinds, called retroviruses, paste a copy of their own instructions into the DNA of the cell that they infect.
Some pieces of DNA, called jumping genes or transposons, can copy themselves and land in a new place. The remains of such pieces make up close to half of all human DNA.
In the 1940s, a scientist named Barbara McClintock studied maize cobs with kernels of many colours and speckles. She worked out that jumping genes could switch a colour gene on and off.

Neanderthals were close cousins of our own species, and they lived in Europe and western Asia until about forty thousand years ago. People with ancestors from outside Africa carry about one or two letters in every hundred from them.
Scientists can now read DNA from bones that are tens of thousands of years old. A small finger bone found in a cave in Siberia revealed an unknown cousin of ours, now called the Denisovans.

In some people, a version of the haemoglobin gene bends the red blood cells into a sickle shape. One copy protects against severe malaria, but two copies cause the serious illness called sickle cell disease.

In sickle cell disease, one letter of the haemoglobin gene has changed, which swaps one building block in the protein. The faulty protein sticks together, and it bends the red blood cells into stiff curves.
Malaria is caused by a tiny parasite that mosquitoes carry from person to person. The parasite lives in red blood cells, and each year it kills hundreds of thousands of people, mostly children.

The sickle version of the gene is most common in parts of Africa, the Mediterranean, the Middle East and India. These are all places where malaria has been common, and the pattern follows the illness rather than any group of people.
Maya found it hard to accept that the same gene version could protect one person and harm another. Teo agreed that it is not fair, and he said that nature has no plan to be fair.
Most babies can digest milk, but in many people the lactase gene switches off in childhood. In some groups with a long history of herding, the gene stays on and adults can drink milk too.
Many adults in Europe and in East Africa can digest milk, but their gene changes are not the same. The same solution appeared more than once, because herding peoples in both places benefited.

The sugar in milk is called lactose, and lactase is the enzyme that breaks it down. Cheese and yoghurt contain less lactose than fresh milk, because microbes use up some of it while the food is being made.
High in the mountains, the air has less oxygen. Many people in Tibet carry a version of a gene called EPAS1 that helps the body cope with it.

People in the Andes and in the highlands of Ethiopia also live in thin air, but their bodies cope in other ways. Scientists think the Tibetan version of EPAS1 may have been inherited from Denisovans, a group of ancient cousins.
No gene works alone in a living body, Teo explained. A gene version is judged by how well it works with all the other genes, just as sugar is judged by the cake.
Many genes act as switches that turn other genes on or off, a little like steps in a recipe. One card sets the next one going, and so a long chain of cards can build a leaf or a heart.
When eggs and sperm are made, the DNA is shuffled, so each one gets a different mix. Because of this, brothers and sisters are alike but never identical, apart from identical twins.

A special kind of division, called meiosis, makes egg and sperm cells that carry only one chromosome from each pair. When an egg and a sperm join, the baby gets a full set of twenty-three pairs again.

For each of the twenty-three pairs, a cell picks one chromosome by chance, as if flipping a coin. That alone gives more than eight million possible combinations in a single parent, before any pieces are swapped.

Teo showed Maya an old photograph of himself with his sister Elena, who is Maya's mother. They had the same parents, but they looked very different, because each had been dealt a different hand of cards.
Because the cards are shuffled in every generation, a gene version keeps meeting new partners. The versions that last are the ones that do well with many different partners, not just one.

Making new combinations is expensive, and scientists still debate why almost all animals do it. One leading idea is that shuffling the cards helps a species to keep one step ahead of fast-changing parasites.
A yeast cell can simply bud, which means that it grows a small copy of itself. Dandelions can also make seeds without any partner, and the young plants are almost exact copies of their parent.
Teo said that each child is like a new hand dealt from two old decks of cards. The cards themselves are very old, but the hand has never been dealt before.

On the wall behind the counter hung a crowd of family photographs, and Maya noticed that she had Rosa's nose. She asked why families look alike, and Teo said that the answer is all about shared cards.
You share about half of your gene versions with each parent, and with each of your own children. A grandparent shares about a quarter, and a first cousin about an eighth.

Any two people share almost all of their DNA, so Teo had to explain what he meant by half. He meant the small number of places where people differ, because there a parent and child match more often than strangers.
Maya drew the family tree on a paper bag and wrote a share beside each person. Her mother Elena got one half, and both her grandmother Rosa and her uncle Teo got one quarter.

Identical twins begin as one fertilised egg that splits into two, so they share almost all of their DNA. Non-identical twins come from two separate eggs, and they share about half, like other brothers and sisters.

In 1964, a young British biologist named William Hamilton worked out something important about helping. A gene that makes animals help their relatives can spread, because those relatives are likely to carry copies of the same gene.
Teo gave the idea a simple rule of thumb, which Maya wrote on the back of a bag. Helping tends to pay off when the benefit to a relative, reduced by how distant that relative is, outweighs the cost.
Rosa wrapped a loaf for her sister Carmen, and Maya laughed and asked whether she was doing the sum. Rosa said that she was doing it out of love, and Teo agreed that the two ideas do not clash.

Ground squirrels sometimes give a loud alarm call when a hawk comes, which warns others but can draw attention to the caller. Researchers found that females with relatives nearby called more often than females without.

Maya studied the photographs again and said that family could not be the whole story. Teo agreed, because animals and people also help friends and strangers, and he promised that they would meet some examples soon.
A mother bird works all day to feed her chicks. Each chick carries about half of her gene versions, so caring for it helps to carry them forward.
Parent blue tits can make hundreds of trips in a single day to carry caterpillars to their nest. Feeding a big family is hard work, and a parent must also save strength for the future.
In a honeybee hive, the workers do not have young of their own. They feed and guard their mother, the queen, because she produces their brothers and sisters.

Dario, who delivers the flour, keeps bees on a hill outside town, and one Saturday he took Maya to see his hives. Teo came too and explained that bee sisters with the same father share about three quarters of their genes.

The picture is not so simple, Dario said, because a honeybee queen mates with about a dozen drones. Most of the workers in the hive are therefore half sisters, who share much less than three quarters.
Not all helping is between relatives, as vampire bats show. They share blood meals with roost mates, and they are more likely to share with bats that once shared with them.
A vampire bat must feed almost every night, and one that goes without food for two or three nights may starve. A bat that has fed well can save a hungry neighbour by sharing some of its blood meal.
Trading favours only works when the same animals meet again and again. If a bat never shares, its roost mates may be less likely to feed it, and then the cheat loses out.
Family members do not always agree about what is fair. A young animal often wants more milk than its mother is ready to give, because she must save strength for her future young.

On Sunday, Maya phoned her mother Elena, who was working far away, and told her all about the bees and the bats. Afterwards she told Teo that a family is both a team and a quarrel, and he said it was mostly a team.
A cuckoo lays an egg in another bird's nest, and the chick pushes the other eggs out. The small birds feed it as if it were their own, although some hosts have learned to spot odd eggs.
A female cuckoo watches from a tree until the small bird leaves, and then she slips into the nest. In only a few seconds, she removes one egg, lays her own and flies away.
Many cuckoo eggs look surprisingly like the eggs of the bird being tricked, with the same colour and spots. A female cuckoo usually lays eggs that match just one kind of host bird.
A young cuckoo is much too big for a reed warbler's nest, but it begs in a special way. Its rapid calls sound like a whole brood of hungry chicks, so the foster parents keep bringing food.
Hosts evolve ways to resist parasites, and parasites evolve ways around those defences. Neither side can stay ahead for very long, so both keep on changing.
Biologists call this the Red Queen effect, after a character in a children's story by Lewis Carroll. In the story, the Red Queen tells Alice that you must run fast just to stay in the same place.
In lakes in New Zealand, scientists studied a small snail that can reproduce either with a partner or on its own. Where parasites were common, a larger share of the snails reproduced with partners.

In tropical forests, a fungus infects carpenter ants and makes them climb a plant and clamp their jaws onto a leaf. The fungus then grows out of the ant and releases spores, which spread to more ants.
Our own bodies are taking part in an arms race with germs as well. Some of the most varied human genes help to recognise germs, and flu viruses change a little every year.
Rosa found a spot of green mould on a forgotten loaf and wrinkled her nose. Maya wrote in her notebook that in nature nobody ever wins for good, because every defence meets a new attack.
Genes do not give orders like the strings of a puppet. They shape how a brain and a body grow, and what we do depends on that growth and on what happens to us.

Every morning, the nurse Ines came into the bakery with her nine-year-old twin sons, Leo and Nico. The boys looked exactly alike, but Leo always chose a bun with raisins and Nico always chose plain bread.
Identical twins start with nearly the same DNA, but they are never exactly alike. Their fingerprints differ, and so do their habits, because chance and life experience matter too.

Teo told Maya that twins differ for many small reasons that add up over the years. A few tiny mutations appear after the egg splits, chance plays a part in growth, and each day brings new experiences.
Cells can add small chemical tags to DNA, which work like pencil notes on a recipe card. A tag can turn a gene up or down without changing a single letter.
A number such as fifty percent heritable is often misunderstood. It does not mean that half of you comes from genes, but that half of the differences in a group are linked to genes.

In many countries, the average person is taller than their great-grandparents were, by many centimetres. The genes of the population hardly changed in so short a time, but food and health care improved a great deal.

Teo said that there is no gene for being a baker, or for being kind, or for telling jokes. Behaviour is shaped by thousands of tiny nudges from the genes, together with everything that happens in life.
Some babies are born with a version of a gene that cannot handle one protein building block. A simple diet that avoids it keeps them healthy, so a gene is not always a fixed fate.

Maya shaped her first whole batch of rolls with her own hands, while Rosa watched and said nothing. She told Teo that genes had given her hands, but she was the one who was learning what to do with them.
Any two people on Earth share roughly 999 letters out of every 1,000. Most of the small differences are found within every group of people, rather than between groups.
Our species is very young, because it is only about three hundred thousand years old. That is a short time for evolution, which is one reason why people everywhere are so alike in their DNA.
Our species began in Africa, and the people who spread to other continents carried only part of its variety. For this reason, Africa holds more genetic variety than any other part of the world.

Features that people notice first, such as skin colour, depend mostly on only a few genes out of about twenty thousand. Skin colour has shifted with the sunlight where families lived, and it says little about the rest of a person.
We share more than 98 out of every 100 DNA letters with chimpanzees. Most of our genes also have a close partner in mice, and many in fruit flies.
Teo drew a branching tree in the flour, with a girl, an ape, a mouse, a fly and yeast at the tips. The more recently two branches split, he said, the more alike their DNA tends to be.

A tiny worm that lives in soil has about twenty thousand genes, which is almost exactly as many as a person has. Rice has even more, so the number of genes does not decide how complicated a living thing is.
To find out what a gene does, scientists often disable it in a fly, a worm or a mouse. Because many of the genes are shared, they can then look for the human version in people with similar problems.

Bacteria can pass small loops of DNA, called plasmids, from one cell to another, even between different kinds. A gene for resisting a medicine can therefore spread sideways, and not only from parent to child.
Maya looked at the tree in the flour and wrote the word cousin beside every tip. Everything alive, from the yeast in the dough to the girl kneading it, was part of one very big family.
Dogs came from wolves many thousands of years ago. People chose which dogs to breed, and in this way they changed the genes of the whole species.

In 1959, a scientist named Dmitri Belyaev began an experiment with foxes on a farm in Siberia. He bred only the tamest foxes from each generation, and within a few generations the pups were wagging their tails.

Cabbage, kale, broccoli and cauliflower all belong to one species, which began as a wild plant growing on seaside cliffs in Europe. Farmers chose plants with big leaves, thick buds or fat flower heads, and they gradually made different vegetables.
Maize was shaped from a wild grass called teosinte in Mexico about nine thousand years ago. Farmers saved seeds from the best plants, season after season, and the gene versions changed.
Rosa's flour comes from bread wheat, which has about five times more DNA than a person has. It has forty-two chromosomes, because it came from three wild grasses that combined their sets.
In 2012, scientists described a tool called CRISPR that can change DNA at a chosen spot. In 2023, a treatment based on it was approved for sickle cell disease.

CRISPR began as a kind of defence that bacteria use against viruses, long before scientists noticed it. Scientists learned to use a short guide strand to lead a cutting protein to a chosen place in DNA.
