The treatment takes blood-making cells from a patient and edits them so that they make the haemoglobin that babies use. The edited cells are then returned to the patient, who needs hospital care before and after.

Changing the cells of one patient affects only that person, but a change in an egg, sperm or embryo would be inherited. For this reason, many countries have strict rules or bans on that kind of editing.
The first human genome took many years and cost billions of dollars. Today, a person's genome can be read in a day or two for a small part of that cost.
Most gene tests show chances, not certainties, so they need to be read carefully. A doctor or a genetic counsellor can explain what a result really means.
Because relatives share gene versions, one person's test can also say something about their family. For this reason, privacy matters, and people should be able to decide who sees their results.
Evolution explains how we came to be the way we are, but it does not tell us how we ought to behave. We can choose to be kind even if no gene tells us to.
Rosa put on her glasses to read a card, and Teo smiled. Glasses, vaccines and medicine all go against what nature would do on its own, and few people think that they are wrong.
People also hand down language, songs, skills and customs, and these are not carried in genes. We are shaped by our genes, but we are also shaped by what we learn from others.

Humans are not the only animals that pass on things that they have learned. Humpback whales pass new songs from one group to the next across the Pacific, and young birds learn their songs from adults.
Every gene in your body has been copied through a very long line of ancestors. Not one of them failed to survive and have young, and the chain goes back billions of years.

You have two parents, four grandparents and eight great-grandparents, and the number doubles with every generation. Thirty generations back, the sum gives more than a billion ancestors, which is far more people than were alive then.

On the final Saturday of the summer, Rosa gave a party, and Teo asked Maya what a gene really is. Maya stood up and said that a gene is a recipe, copied and tested in a body, which never wants anything.
Maya wrote a card for a new bread and slid it into the box beside Rosa's old ones. Teo smiled and said that she herself was a new edition of a very old book.
C1C2: On the first morning of the summer, Maya found a worn wooden box of handwritten recipe cards at the back of her grandmother Rosa's bakery. Her uncle Teo, who taught biology, looked at the cards and smiled, because he said that every living thing carries a box very much like this one. By the end of the summer, he promised, she would know exactly what he meant.

Rosa came over, wiping the flour from her hands, and told Maya that the box had belonged to her own mother. Over many years the cards had been copied out by hand again and again, and some of them were older than Rosa herself. Maya turned them over carefully, noticing the stains, the crossed-out words and the tiny notes squeezed into the margins.

Maya asked what on earth he meant by that, and Teo only laughed, because the full answer, he said, would take the whole summer. So he proposed a bargain in which she could ask one question every day while they worked, and he would answer it as honestly as he could. Maya fetched an empty notebook from her bag and wrote the date at the top of the first page, feeling that something important had begun.

Teo held up a single card and pointed out that a recipe does not bake a loaf by itself, since it only tells a baker what to do. A gene is the same kind of thing, he said, a set of instructions for building one useful part of a living body. It still needs a kitchen full of busy workers to carry those instructions out.

Rosa's card for plain bread was short and simple, naming only four ingredients: flour, water, salt and yeast. Yet the steps mattered as much as the list, because the dough had to be mixed, rested, shaped and baked in just the right order. Teo observed that a gene, too, is not merely a list of parts but a sequence in which the order carries the meaning.

Rosa showed Maya two loaves that she had baked from exactly the same card on different days, and they were not quite alike. One was darker and taller because the oven had run hotter, while the other was paler because the morning air was damp. Teo said that the card was only part of the story, since what comes out of any kitchen also depends on the conditions in which the recipe is carried out.

Teo explained that the body is built from trillions of tiny rooms called cells, and that each of them works like a very small, very busy kitchen. Almost every cell keeps a full copy of the family recipe box, tucked safely inside a central compartment called the nucleus. A single cell will only use a few of the cards at a time, however, and leaves all the rest on the shelf.

Rosa never carried the precious old cards into the busy kitchen, where flour, butter and steam would soon have ruined them. Instead she made a copy of the card she needed and handed it to the baker, leaving the original safe in the office. Teo said that a cell works in just the same way, keeping its original recipes safe in the nucleus and sending out working copies to the cooks.

Maya wondered whether every single cell really holds a copy of the box, and Teo admitted that there are a few exceptions. A mature red blood cell in the human body has no nucleus at all, having discarded its recipes while it was growing up. This leaves the whole cell free to be packed with the protein that carries oxygen, and it can go on doing its job for a few months without any cards.

At last Teo gave the cards their proper scientific name, which was genes, a word that Maya repeated twice to herself. Maya opened her new notebook and wrote down, in her neatest handwriting, that a gene is a recipe for making one useful thing. Beneath it she added a question for the next day, and she noticed that she was already looking forward to finding out the answer.

Rosa's cards were written in ink, but the cards in a cell are written in DNA, a long molecule twisted into the shape of a spiral ladder. Its alphabet has only four letters, called A, C, G and T, which is far fewer than the letters of our own alphabet. It is the order in which they appear that carries all of the meaning.

To make the idea easier to see, Rosa baked biscuits in the shapes of the letters A, C, G and T, and Teo arranged them in rows on a tray. He pointed out that a computer writes every photograph and song with just two symbols, so four letters strung into a very long chain can certainly carry a great deal of information. What matters, he said, is not how many letters there are but the order in which they are arranged.

Teo took two ribbons and laid them side by side to show that the DNA ladder has two long sides, joined by rungs that are each made of a pair of letters. The pairing follows a strict rule, in which A always sits opposite T and C always sits opposite G, and nothing else ever fits. It is a little like a lock and a key, where only the right piece will ever slide into place.

This pairing rule has a remarkable consequence, which is that each side of the ladder is a mirror image of the other. Anyone who knows the letters along one side can therefore write out the letters along the opposite side without ever seeing it. Teo said that this simple fact is the secret behind the way DNA is copied, and he promised to explain it when the time was right.

Nobody had seen the shape of DNA until 1953, when scientists in Cambridge worked out that it forms a double spiral. They relied on clues from X-ray photographs, and the clearest of those pictures had been taken by Rosalind Franklin and her colleagues. The whole ladder is only about two billionths of a metre across, which makes it tens of thousands of times thinner than a human hair.

Whenever a cell needs a particular gene, it first makes a temporary copy of that gene on a thin strand called RNA, which is rather like a photocopy of a recipe card. The copy slips out of the nucleus and travels to the cooks in the rest of the cell. Meanwhile the original DNA stays where it is, protected from the heat, the splashes and the general bustle of the kitchen.

Inside the cell, machines read the DNA letters in groups of three, a little like reading a sentence word by word. Each group picks out one building block from a set of twenty called amino acids. The machines then join those blocks into a chain in exactly the order that the gene demands.

Four letters taken three at a time can be arranged in sixty-four different ways, yet the cell has only twenty kinds of building block to choose from. The code therefore has some spare capacity, and several different words often point to the very same block. Teo compared this to a language that has many words for one thing, such as sofa, couch and settee.

Reading does not begin just anywhere along the strand, because a special start word marks the place where a gene begins. A stop word, which stands for no building block at all, tells the cell that the chain is complete and the work can end. Teo likened these two signals to the first and last lines of a recipe, which tell a cook exactly where to begin and where to finish.

Teo told Maya that the three-letter dictionary is almost identical in bananas, bacteria, mushrooms and people, with only a few small exceptions. It is as though every living thing on Earth had agreed on the same language long ago, and nobody has ever needed to change it much. This is why a gene from one species can often be read and used by the cells of another, a fact that scientists use in medicine every day.

Once a chain of amino acids is finished, it folds itself into a precise shape, and we call the result a protein. Proteins are the real workers of the body, because some build hair and skin and some digest your lunch. One of them, called haemoglobin, carries oxygen around in the blood to every part of the body.

A finished chain does not stay straight for long, because it folds itself up into a precise and intricate shape, rather as pastry is folded into layers. That shape decides the protein's job, in the same way that the shape of a key decides which lock it can open. If even one building block is wrong, the fold can go astray, and the protein may then work badly or not at all.

Many proteins are simply building materials, rather like the bricks, beams and tiles of a house. Keratin is the tough protein that forms hair and nails, while collagen is a strong, rope-like protein that gives strength to skin, bones and tendons. A great deal of the body, in other words, is made of proteins that were first written as instructions on a recipe card.

Maya chewed a crust of bread for a full minute while Teo watched, and she noticed that it began to taste faintly sweet. A protein called amylase, which the body makes from the instructions of a gene, was cutting the long chains of starch into small sugars. Proteins that speed up a job in this way are called enzymes, and the body relies on thousands of them.

The protein haemoglobin is what makes blood red, because every molecule of it holds atoms of iron. In the lungs the iron grabs hold of oxygen, and in the muscles and brain it lets go again, rather like a delivery van that collects and drops off its load. Because haemoglobin is built from instructions in the genes, a change in those instructions can change how well the delivery works.

Yeast, the secret of every loaf, is a tiny single-celled fungus with a recipe box of its own. Its genes build the enzymes that break down sugar, and a leftover from the process is carbon dioxide gas, which puffs the dough up with thousands of bubbles. In the corner stood Rosa's old jar of sourdough starter, which she called Bernardo, and which was a bubbling crowd of billions of yeast cells and friendly bacteria.

A yeast cell has about six thousand genes, far fewer than the twenty thousand or so in a human cell. Even so, some of those genes are so old that scientists have swapped a human gene into a yeast cell and found that it worked. Teo said that this was one of the best clues that people and baker's yeast, for all their differences, share a very distant ancestor.

Proteins do not last forever, because they wear out, and the cell breaks them up and reuses the parts. This means that the cards have to be read over and over again, just as Rosa's bread card was used every single morning of the year. A cell is never finished with its recipes, since the cooking goes on for as long as the body is alive.

Teo explained that a cell can sometimes read a single gene in more than one way, leaving out a few pieces or keeping them, and so produce several slightly different proteins. It is like a card for a basic dough that can be turned into a loaf, a roll or a pizza base depending on what is added. This is one reason why the human body contains many more kinds of protein than it has genes.

At the end of the first week, Maya filled a whole page of her notebook with a summary of everything she had learned so far. DNA holds the recipes, RNA carries a copy of one recipe out to the cooks, and proteins are the workers that build and run the body. Teo read it twice and said that she had just described how almost every living thing on Earth works.

In every human cell there are about three billion letters of DNA, and about 20,000 of the genes that make proteins. If you could pull the DNA from a single cell into a straight line, it would stretch for roughly two metres. Yet it is folded so cleverly that it fits inside a space far smaller than a speck of dust.

Teo asked Maya to imagine reading all three billion letters aloud, one every second, day and night, without ever stopping for a rest. It would take her roughly a hundred years to reach the end, and even then she would have read only one set of the instructions. Almost every cell in the body holds two sets, one from each parent, so the real library is twice as long.

The long thread of DNA does not float loose in the nucleus, because it is wound around tiny spools made of proteins called histones. These spools are then coiled and folded, again and again, until the whole thread is packed into a very small space, a little like cotton in a well-organised sewing box. The packing does more than save room, since it also helps to decide which parts of the thread can be reached and read.

To keep the long threads tidy, the DNA is wound into bundles called chromosomes, and a human cell has 23 pairs of them. One chromosome in each pair came from your mother and the other from your father. In a literal sense, then, you are a mixture of two family recipe boxes.

Twenty-two of the pairs are simply numbered, but the twenty-third pair is special, because it helps to decide a baby's sex. Usually a girl has two chromosomes called X, while a boy has one X and one much smaller chromosome called Y. A single gene on the Y chromosome normally starts the chain of events that makes a baby develop as a boy, which shows how much one card can do.

Only about one or two letters in every hundred belong to the genes that make proteins, which comes as a surprise to most people. Some of the rest has other jobs, and some of it may do nothing useful at all, and scientists still argue about how much of it falls into each group. Teo warned Maya never to call it rubbish, because several parts once thought to be useless later turned out to matter.

Genes come in very different sizes, from a few hundred letters to more than two million. The longest human gene is like a recipe card so long that it would stretch right across the kitchen, and the cell has to copy all of it every time the gene is read. Teo said that a short card is not a weak card, since a gene's importance has nothing to do with how long it is.

Maya wondered how one box of recipes could make both a heart cell and a skin cell, and Teo told her that the cells simply use different cards. Much of our DNA does not make proteins at all but works as a set of switches. These decide which genes are turned on, where in the body, and at what moment.

Every person began life as a single cell, which divided into two, then four, then eight, and went on dividing until there were tens of trillions. Each new cell kept the same recipe box, yet as the cells multiplied they began to use different cards and settled into different jobs, as muscle, nerve, skin or blood. Maya found it hard to believe that her whole body, and her wiggling toes, had grown from a speck no bigger than a grain of sand.

Outside the nucleus, most cells also hold hundreds of small power stations called mitochondria, and each one carries a tiny circle of DNA of its own, with only thirty-seven genes. Scientists think that these power stations were once free-living bacteria that moved into a larger cell more than a billion years ago and never left. A child normally receives all of its mitochondria from its mother, because the egg supplies them and the sperm does not.

Long before anyone had seen DNA, a monk named Gregor Mendel spent years in the 1860s growing and counting pea plants in a monastery garden. He noticed that features such as tall or short stems were handed on in separate units rather than blending like paint. His careful patterns were later recognised as the first clear evidence that genes exist.

Mendel chose peas for good reasons, because they grow quickly in a garden and each plant produces a great many seeds. Their features also come in clear either-or pairs, such as tall or short stems, round or wrinkled seeds, and purple or white flowers. A plant with half-way features would have made his counting much harder, so the clear choices were a gift.

To control which plants became parents, Mendel carried pollen from one flower to another with a small brush, and he protected the flowers so that no insect could interfere. This meant that he knew exactly which two plants had produced every single seed. Without such care, his results might have been a muddle, and we might never have heard of him.

When Mendel crossed a tall pea plant with a short one, every single plant in the next generation turned out to be tall. The short feature seemed to have vanished completely, as though it had never existed in the family at all. Mendel could easily have stopped there, but he was curious enough to wonder where the missing feature had gone.

Next he allowed the tall plants of the new generation to pollinate themselves, and the short feature suddenly reappeared. It turned up in about one plant out of every four, which meant that there were roughly three tall plants for every short one. The same ratio, close to three to one, showed up again and again in other features, whether he was counting seeds, flowers or pods.

Mendel reasoned that every plant must hold two units for each feature, one received from each parent, and that one of the two could hide the other. A short plant's unit could therefore lie unseen for a whole generation and then reappear, unchanged, when two hidden copies came together. It was a brilliant guess, made long before anyone could see anything of the kind.

Most people at the time imagined that the features of two parents blended together like paint poured into the same pot, so that every child was a smooth mixture. Mendel's peas showed something quite different, because the units never melted into one another and could come back, as good as new, after a generation in hiding. Recipe cards behave in just the same way, said Teo, since a card for cake and a card for bread never merge into one card for both.

Mendel was a patient man, and his experiments lasted about eight years, during which he grew and counted many thousands of plants. Such large numbers mattered, because a pattern seen in a handful of plants might easily be chance, while one seen in thousands is much harder to dismiss. His notes, written in neat columns, still impress scientists who read them today, more than a century and a half later.

Mendel published his results in 1866 in a journal of his local society, and then almost nobody took any notice. He became the head of his monastery, and he died in 1884 without ever knowing how important his work would become. It was not until about 1900 that several scientists rediscovered it and understood that he had found the basic rules of heredity.

Maya wrote Mendel's name at the top of a fresh page of her notebook, and underneath she noted that he had discovered the rules without ever seeing a gene. Teo smiled and said that careful counting can reveal a pattern long before anyone understands the machinery that lies behind it. Maya decided there and then that she would be a counter and a questioner, and she began by counting the loaves that sold before nine o'clock.

Teo laid two cards side by side that described the same cake but called for different amounts of sugar. In the same way, a gene can exist in several slightly different versions, which scientists sometimes call alleles. Since you inherit one copy from each parent, you may carry two different versions of the same gene.

Scientists have since found out what Mendel's wrinkled peas were hiding, which is one faulty version of a gene for an enzyme that builds starch. Seeds with only faulty copies hold too much sugar and too little starch, and so they shrink and wrinkle as they dry. A round pea has at least one working copy, which is enough to make the starch and keep the seed smooth.

When a single copy of a gene is enough to show a feature, scientists call that version dominant, and the version that is hidden beside it is called recessive. A hidden copy does not vanish, though, because a parent can pass it on to a child without ever showing it. If the child also receives a hidden copy from the other parent, the feature that nobody has seen for generations can suddenly come back.

Red hair is a good example, because it usually appears only when a child receives a particular version of one gene from both parents. Two parents with brown hair may each carry a hidden copy, and then each of their children has about one chance in four of having red hair. Teo added that hair colour is a bit more complicated than that, but the basic picture is a useful one.

Teo drew a square of four boxes in the spilled flour, with the copies of one parent written along the top and those of the other parent down the side. Each box showed one way in which a pair of copies could meet in a child, and every box was equally likely. If two parents each carried one hidden copy, one box out of four would show the hidden feature and the other three would not.

A few features follow Mendel's neat rules quite closely, and the ABO blood group is one of them. It depends mainly on a single gene that has three common versions, which are called A, B and O. Teo said that such tidy cases are the exception, however, and that most of the features people care about are much messier.

Teo warned Maya that headlines about a gene for this or a gene for that are almost always an oversimplification. Height, for instance, is influenced by thousands of tiny differences scattered across the DNA. Food, health and chance during growing up also play their part in the final result.

In the pantry there was a doorframe covered in pencil marks, each showing how tall one of the family's children had been on a birthday long ago. Maya stood against it and found that she was close to her mother's mark at the same age, though not quite the same. Teo said that children often land near their parents, but that brothers and sisters usually land in different places.

Teo asked Maya to think of height as a recipe made of thousands of small pinches, each of which adds or takes away a tiny amount. Because there are so many pinches, each person's total falls somewhere along a smooth range, and most people end up near the middle with only a few at either extreme. This is also why a single gene is a poor guide to who will be tall, since each of the thousands does so little.

Even eye colour, which looks so simple, turns out to be shaped by several genes, with one or two of them doing most of the work. That is why two blue-eyed parents can occasionally have a child with a different eye colour, and why textbooks that once taught a single-gene rule have been rewritten. Maya summed it up in her notebook by writing that the cards are handed on whole, but their effects can combine in many ways.

Maya scraped her finger on the edge of a baking tin, and within a week the cut had almost disappeared. Teo explained that cells beside the wound had been dividing to fill the gap, and every new cell needed its own complete copy of the recipe box. Growing, healing and replacing worn-out parts all depend on this endless copying, which goes on in everybody's body at every moment of the day.

Teo asked Maya to imagine copying out thousands of thick novels by hand, because that is about how many letters a cell must copy each time it divides. Rosa laughed and said that she made mistakes even when she copied a single card, so she would never survive such a task. A cell, however, does it in a matter of hours and makes astonishingly few errors.

When a cell is about to divide, it unzips its long ladder of DNA down the middle and builds a new matching half for each side. Proofreading proteins check the new strand as it grows, rather like a baker rereading a card before it goes into the box. As a result, errors are extremely rare, though of course they are not quite impossible.

One machine copying from one end to the other would take far too long, so the cell does not work that way. It begins the copying at thousands of places along the thread at once, and teams of copying proteins move outward in both directions until they meet. It is rather like a hundred bakers each making a single tray, instead of one baker making the whole day's bread alone.

The main copying machine is a protein with the long name of DNA polymerase. It slides along one opened side of the ladder and, for every letter it meets, it adds the matching partner: a T opposite each A, a G opposite each C. When it has finished, each of the two new ladders is made of one old side and one brand new side.

The copying machine does not simply add letters and move on, because it checks each new letter the moment it is in place. If a wrong letter has slipped in, the machine backs up a step, cuts the mistake out and tries again, much as a baker scrapes off a badly piped line of icing and starts over. This proofreading catches the great majority of the errors before the machine has moved on, which is why the finished copy is so accurate.

When the copying is finished, a second team of proteins goes along the new strand looking for letters that do not match their partners, and it repairs those that it finds. After all this care, only about one letter in a billion, or even fewer, is left wrong. That is roughly the same as a copyist who types a whole library and leaves behind only a handful of misprints.

Every second, the human body makes about two million new red blood cells, and the outer layer of skin renews itself roughly once a month. Behind all of this renewal, cells in the bone marrow and the skin are copying their DNA again and again, day and night. Maya looked at her hands and tried to imagine the quiet, ceaseless copying going on beneath the freckles.

Not every cell in the body keeps on copying itself and dividing, and Teo told Maya that most nerve cells stop early in life. They are built to last for many years instead of being replaced, rather like the stone walls of a house. Skin and blood cells, which face daily wear and tear, are replaced constantly, and so they must copy their DNA more often.

One mistake in a billion letters sounds almost perfect, but a cell holds billions of letters, and the body holds trillions of cells, and the copying goes on for a lifetime. Teo said that some mistakes are therefore bound to slip through, however good the proofreaders may be. That, he promised, was where the story of the box became truly interesting, and he suggested that Maya should come back for the next lesson with an open mind.

Every so often a mistake slips past the proofreaders, and a letter in the DNA is swapped, lost or added, which is what scientists call a mutation. Each person is born with a few dozen brand new mutations that neither of their parents had. Almost all of them are far too small to notice, and most do no harm at all.

Teo wrote a sentence made only of three-letter words on a card: THE CAT SAW THE DOG. When he swapped a single letter, it became THE CAR SAW THE DOG, and only one word had changed, so the damage was easy to see and small. A swap of this kind is often among the gentlest sorts of mutation, because the rest of the message is still readable.

Then he added one extra letter, a Z, after the first word, and read the sentence again in groups of three: THE ZCA TSA WTH EDO G. Every word after the mistake was ruined, because the extra letter had shifted the whole reading frame by one place. Inside a gene, a mutation that adds or removes one or two letters is usually far more damaging for this reason.

Teo said that most mutations are like a smudge on a recipe card, where the cake comes out the same anyway. A few do harm, and a very small number turn out to be useful. The crucial point is that mutations happen by chance and are not designed to solve whatever problem the living thing faces.

Because several different words can stand for the same building block, many swaps are silent, and the finished protein turns out exactly as it would have done without them. This is especially common when the third letter of a word changes, which is why Teo called the third letter often the least important part of each word. Such mutations are like a baker misspelling the word dough on a card, where everybody still knows what the word means.

A few mutations change an important building block or scramble the reading of a gene, and then the protein cannot do its job properly. Some of these changes cause illnesses, and those that are carried in egg or sperm cells can be passed on in families. Teo spoke gently about this, saying that scientists study such changes mainly in order to find ways of helping people who are affected.

On the pale sandy beaches of Florida live small mice that carry changes in genes for coat colour, which make their fur much lighter than that of their dark cousins on the mainland. On light sand, predators such as owls find these pale mice harder to spot, so the change helps them. The same change would be a handicap on dark soil, which is why Teo said that a mutation is rarely good or bad in itself, only good or bad in a place.

Most mutations come from small copying mistakes, but DNA can also be damaged by things from outside the body. Ultraviolet rays in strong sunlight and some chemicals in tobacco smoke are two well-known examples, and a skin cell is surprisingly good at repairing the harm. This is one reason why many doctors advise people to protect their skin from strong sun.

A mutation in a skin or muscle cell stays within that one body, and it comes to an end when the person's life does. Only a change in an egg cell or a sperm cell can be handed on to a child, and so only those changes matter for the long story of heredity. Teo added that some changes in body cells can cause problems for the person, and the body has many ways of checking for them.

Maya sat very still for a moment, because she had just noticed something that surprised her a great deal. Every different version of every gene, in every living thing, must once have begun as a mistake in a single cell. Without those rare accidents all the cards would be identical, and the story of life would have had nothing to work with.

Because new mutations keep appearing, and because each parent passes on a different mix, the cards in a population drift slowly apart. Every group of living things therefore holds a rich supply of small differences between its members. Teo said that this variety is the raw material for everything that follows in the story of life.

Rosa's younger sister Carmen kept her own copy of the family cake card, and when the two cards were laid side by side, they were not quite the same. Each time the card had been copied by hand, somebody had changed a little of it, a spoonful of this or a pinch of that. The versions that tasted best had been copied again and again, while the disappointing ones had quietly been forgotten.

Every living thing makes more offspring than the world has room for, so some survive and have young while others do not. When the differences are inherited, the versions that help are copied into the next generation more often. Charles Darwin called this process natural selection, and he described it long before anyone knew about genes.

A cod can lay millions of eggs in a single year, and a mature oak tree can drop many thousands of acorns. If they all grew up, the sea and the land would soon be crowded with nothing but cod and oaks, yet almost none of them do. Which ones survive is never entirely a matter of luck, because even small differences in strength, speed or hardiness can tip the balance.

In 1977 a severe drought struck a small island in the Galapagos, and the small, soft seeds that finches prefer soon ran out. Only the large, hard seeds were left, and the birds with deeper, stronger beaks were better at cracking them, so more of those birds survived. When the next chicks hatched, their beaks were deeper on average, because beak size is largely passed on in the genes.

Teo gave a modern example that can be seen within days, which was bacteria meeting an antibiotic. Bacteria can divide every twenty minutes or so, and if just a few happen to carry a version that resists the medicine, they survive and multiply. Soon nearly all of the bacteria are resistant, and the old medicine no longer works.

In 1928 a scientist named Alexander Fleming returned from a holiday and noticed a clear ring around a patch of mould on a dish of bacteria. The mould was making a substance that killed the bacteria nearby, and over the following years this discovery grew into the first widely used antibiotic, penicillin. Antibiotics have saved countless lives since then, which is exactly why it matters so much that bacteria are learning to resist them.

Every time an antibiotic is used, any bacteria that can resist it have a better chance of surviving and spreading, because their competitors have been cleared away. That is why doctors ask people to use these medicines only when they are really needed, and to follow the advice that they are given. Teo stressed that this is general information about how resistance spreads and not a substitute for a doctor's guidance.

Natural selection has no planner and no goal, and nobody stands behind it making the choices. It behaves rather like Rosa's flour sieve, which keeps whatever happens to be the right size and lets everything else fall away. Because it can only work with the versions that already exist, it seldom produces a perfect answer, only one that works well enough.

That evening Maya wrote in her notebook that the cards found in living things today are the survivors of an enormously long process of copying. Those that were copied well were still in the box, while the others had simply disappeared along the way. Teo nodded slowly and said that she had just understood one of the biggest ideas in the whole of biology.

Bodies do not last, Teo said, but the instructions can be copied from one generation to the next for thousands of years. Seen from that angle, a gene version that helps its bodies survive and breed will tend to become more common. Over time, the genes we find in living things are therefore the ones that were good at being copied.

When biologists say that a gene version is useful, they mean only that it helps the bodies that carry it to survive and have young. By that measure a gene succeeds whenever copies of it reach the next generation, and it fails whenever they do not. Every card in the box today therefore belongs to a long line of successes, since the failures left no copies behind to be counted.

One of the histone proteins that wrap up DNA is almost exactly the same in a pea plant and in a cow, differing in only two of its building blocks. Yet plants and animals went their separate ways more than a billion years ago, and in all that time very little about this protein has changed. When a card is so important that almost any change spoils it, selection tends to keep the old version safe.

Teo stopped and said that the language they had been using could mislead, because genes do not think, plan or want anything. When biologists say that a gene wants to spread, they mean only that gene versions which happen to be copied well are the ones still around. In the same way, a river does not want to reach the sea, but it gets there all the same.

Rosa listened to the conversation from behind the counter and said that she had never once thought of a recipe wanting to be baked. And yet, she admitted, the cards that people loved were used again and again, while the ones nobody liked had long since sunk to the bottom of the box. Teo said that this was exactly the point, because no wish is needed for the useful cards to become common.

Teo pointed to the old stone bridge at the end of the street and said that it had survived because it was built well, while weaker ones had fallen down. What we see today is therefore never a fair sample of everything that was ever made, only of what lasted. Genes are the same, because the ones we find in living things are the ones whose copies kept going, and the rest have left no trace.

A gene cannot reach the next generation on its own, because it travels inside a body that must survive and have young. Every gene is therefore tested by how well the body it helps to build gets on in the world, rather as a recipe is tested by the loaf that comes out of the oven. Teo said that this is why genes that build healthy bodies in a given place tend to be the ones that last in that place.

Evolution never starts again from a clean sheet, so it can only change what already exists, bit by bit. The human eye shows this well, because its nerve fibres run in front of the light-sensitive layer and then pass through it, leaving a small blind spot. The eye of an octopus evolved separately and is wired the other way round, so it has no such blind spot at all.

The Earth is about four and a half billion years old, and there are signs of life in rocks that are more than three billion years old. That is an almost unimaginable length of time, and it gives even the tiniest changes a chance to add up. Teo asked Maya to imagine taking one step for every thousand years of life, and she worked out that the walk would be over two thousand kilometres long.

Halfway through the summer, on a warm evening after the shop had closed, Maya read her notebook aloud to Rosa from the first page to the last. It told of recipes and workers, of careful copying and rare mistakes, and of the survivors that had been copied through the ages. When she had finished, Rosa wiped her eyes with her apron and said that her own mother would have loved to hear every word.

In July, a cloud of tiny fruit flies gathered above a bowl of overripe bananas, and Rosa flapped her cloth at them in despair. Teo gently stopped her and explained that for more than a hundred years, scientists have kept these flies in laboratories, because they breed fast and are easy to look after. A surprising amount of what we know about genes was first discovered in those humble insects.

Some genes are astonishingly old, because their cards were copied before flies, fish and humans went their separate ways. One family, called the Hox genes, helps to decide which body parts grow where along the length of an animal. Fruit flies and people have versions of them that look surprisingly alike, even though the animals look so different.

In one famous mutant fly, a changed Hox gene had caused a pair of legs to grow on the head, in the place where the antennae should have been. The gene does not build a leg itself, but acts like a manager, telling a group of cells which structure to make. It was a striking sign that a single card can switch on a whole sequence of other cards.

Now and then a mistake in copying makes a spare copy of an entire gene, so that a body ends up with two copies of the same card. One copy carries on with the old job, while the spare is free to change and may eventually learn a new one. Our haemoglobin genes grew from a single ancestor in just this way, which is why several of them look like cousins.

Scientists have discovered that about eight of every hundred letters in human DNA are the remains of viruses that infected our distant ancestors. Most of these pieces are silent now, as if they were cards that nobody uses any more. A few, however, have been put to use, and one of them seems to help a baby's placenta to form.

A virus is a tiny package of instructions that tricks a cell into building more viruses. Some kinds, called retroviruses, paste a copy of their own instructions into the DNA of the cell that they infect. If that happens in an egg or a sperm cell, the pasted piece can be inherited by a child, and then by the child's children, for as long as the family lasts.

Some pieces of DNA, known as jumping genes or transposons, are able to copy themselves and land in a new place along the thread. Their old remains make up close to half of all human DNA, though most of them have long since lost the ability to move. They are another reason why a genome is not a neat book but more like a well-used family notebook, full of additions and scribbles.

In the 1940s a scientist named Barbara McClintock studied maize plants whose kernels were speckled with spots of many colours. She worked out that a jumping piece of DNA could land in a colour gene and switch it off, and then jump out again so that the colour came back. Many of her colleagues found the idea hard to accept at first, but she was given a Nobel Prize for it in 1983.

Neanderthals were close cousins of our own species, and they lived in Europe and western Asia until about forty thousand years ago. When early modern humans met them, the two groups sometimes had children together, and as a result people with ancestors from outside Africa carry about one or two letters in every hundred from them. Some of those inherited pieces influence things such as how the body responds to germs.

Scientists have learned to read DNA from bones that are tens of thousands of years old, which is a little like reading a recipe from a card that has been buried for ages. A small finger bone found in a cave in Siberia revealed a previously unknown group of human cousins, now called the Denisovans. Maya wrote in her notebook that the box is not only a set of recipes but also a history book, and Teo said that was exactly right.

A change in the gene for haemoglobin can bend red blood cells into a sickle shape, and a person with two copies of it suffers from sickle cell disease. Someone with just one copy is better protected against severe malaria, a dangerous illness spread by mosquitoes. That explains why the version stays common in places where malaria has been a danger, even though it carries a cost.

In sickle cell disease, one letter of the haemoglobin gene has changed, and that swaps a single building block in the protein for another. When oxygen is low, the faulty haemoglobin sticks together in stiff rods that bend the red blood cell out of shape. The bent cells can block tiny blood vessels and wear out quickly, which causes pain and tiredness in people who have the illness.

Malaria is caused by a tiny parasite that mosquitoes carry from one person to another. The parasite spends part of its life inside red blood cells, and even today the illness kills hundreds of thousands of people every year, most of them young children. Where malaria has been common for thousands of years, anything that helps a child to survive it can spread through the population.

The sickle version of the gene is most common in parts of Africa, the Mediterranean, the Middle East and India, and in people whose families came from those places. What these regions share is a long history of malaria, so the pattern follows the illness and not any single group of people. Teo stressed that the pattern reflects the places where families have lived, and that it has nothing to do with one kind of person being better or worse than another.

Maya found it hard to accept that the very same gene version could protect one person and make another one ill. Teo agreed that it did not seem fair, and he reminded her that natural selection has no plan and no sense of justice. It simply keeps whatever leaves more copies behind, even when the price is paid by some of the children born along the way.

Almost all babies can digest milk because a gene called the lactase gene is switched on, but in most of the world's adults it switches off in childhood. In some groups whose ancestors kept cattle, a change spread in the past several thousand years that keeps the gene on. Adults in those groups can therefore drink milk without any trouble, although most people in the world cannot.

Many adults in northern Europe and in parts of East Africa can digest milk, but when scientists compared their DNA, they found that the changes were not the same. Different mutations near the lactase gene had appeared independently in each region, and each one had spread because cattle herders who could use fresh milk did well. It is rather like two bakers in two towns who, without ever meeting, both invent the same improvement to the same loaf.

The sugar in milk is called lactose, and lactase is the enzyme that breaks it down, which is why the gene has that name. Cheese and yoghurt contain much less lactose than fresh milk, because friendly microbes use some of it up while the food is being made. Teo suggested that early farmers who could not digest fresh milk may have discovered cheese and yoghurt long before the lactase change became common.

On the high plateau of Tibet, the air holds much less oxygen than at sea level, and most visitors soon feel tired and breathless. Many people living there carry a particular version of a gene called EPAS1, which is rare in most other places. Scientists think it helps their bodies to cope with the thin air without making their blood too thick.

People in the Andes and in the highlands of Ethiopia also live in thin air, but their bodies seem to cope with it in different ways, using different genes. In Tibet, scientists think the helpful version of EPAS1 may have been inherited from the Denisovans, the ancient cousins who left their DNA in a few modern populations. Teo said that there are many routes up the same mountain, and that selection can follow any route that happens to be open.

A gene is never tested alone, Teo explained, because it always works alongside thousands of others in the same body. A version that is excellent in one body, with one set of partners, may be useless in another. In the same way, a spoonful of salt may rescue one recipe and ruin a different one.

Many genes act as switches that turn other genes on or off, so that the cards in the box form long chains and networks. One card sets the next one going, which sets off another, in the way that a good recipe tells you to start the icing only when the cake has cooled. By linking many cards into a sequence like this, a body can build something as complicated as a heart or a leaf from a set of simple instructions.

When an egg or a sperm cell is made, the chromosomes in each pair swap pieces and are dealt out again, so no two cells contain exactly the same mixture. This is why brothers and sisters resemble each other without being exact copies of one another. Each new person is a fresh combination of genes that has never been seen before.

Teo explained that egg and sperm cells are made by a special kind of division, called meiosis, which gives each of them only one chromosome from every pair. When an egg and a sperm join, the new cell has a full set of twenty-three pairs again, half of them from the mother and half from the father. That single cell is where every new person begins, and it already holds the whole recipe box.

Maya took twenty-three coins from the till and flipped them one by one, each coin standing for a pair of chromosomes and each result for the chromosome that was chosen. Teo told her that this chance alone allows more than eight million different combinations in a single parent, before any swapping of pieces has even begun. When both parents are counted, the number of possible children becomes far too big for anyone to picture.

Teo showed Maya an old photograph of himself standing beside his sister Elena, who is Maya's mother. They had grown up in the same house with the same parents, and yet they looked quite different, because each of them had been dealt a different hand of cards from the same two boxes. Maya laughed and said that her mother and her uncle seemed to share nothing except a love of bread.

Since the cards are shuffled in every generation, a gene version never gets to keep the same partners for long, and it must do its job well alongside many different companions. A card that works brilliantly only with one particular partner will soon be separated from it, and so it tends to fade away. This is why the versions that last are generally the good all-rounders, the sort of ingredients that improve almost any recipe.

Why sexual reproduction exists is still a lively question, because it costs a great deal of energy compared with simple copying. One popular idea is that shuffling the genes helps a species to stay ahead of parasites, which evolve very quickly. Biologists agree, however, that no single explanation covers every case that we know about.

Many living things manage perfectly well without sex, and a yeast cell can simply bud, growing a small copy of itself. Many dandelions make seeds without any partner, so that the young plants are almost exact copies of their parent. Rosa's jar of Bernardo was mostly a crowd of such copies, although Teo added that yeast can mate when times are hard, which is one of the puzzles that biologists like to argue about.

Teo summed up the week by saying that each child is like a new hand dealt from two old decks of cards. The cards themselves are very old, and some of them are millions of years old, but the particular hand has never been dealt before, and apart from identical twins it will never be dealt again. Maya thought that this was a good reason for treating every person as someone truly new.

On the wall behind the counter hung a crowd of framed family photographs, and Maya noticed with a shock that she had Rosa's nose. She asked why members of a family so often look alike, and Teo replied that the answer lay in how many of the same cards they share. He took down a photograph of four generations of women and began to count.

On average, you share about half of your gene versions with each parent, each child and each brother or sister. The share halves with each step further out, so a grandparent or an uncle shares about a quarter. A first cousin shares about an eighth, which is why families really do look alike.

Maya objected that everybody shares almost all of their DNA, so Teo explained what he meant by half. He was counting only the small number of places where people differ, because at those places a parent and child match each other much more often than two strangers do. Relatedness, in other words, is a measure of shared differences against a background that nearly everyone has in common.

Maya drew the family tree on a paper bag and wrote a fraction beside each person. Her mother Elena received one half, while her grandmother Rosa and her uncle Teo each received one quarter, and Teo said that these numbers were averages rather than exact counts. Because the cards are shuffled, any real person might share a little more or a little less than the average.

Identical twins begin as a single fertilised egg that splits into two, and so they share almost exactly the same DNA. Non-identical twins, by contrast, grow from two separate eggs, and they share about half of their gene versions on average, just like any other brothers and sisters. Teo said that identical twins are therefore the closest relatives that two people can possibly be.

In 1964, a young British biologist named William Hamilton worked out a clear way of thinking about family helpfulness. If a gene makes an animal help its relatives, then the gene can spread, because those relatives have a good chance of carrying copies of the very same gene. Teo called this one of the neatest ideas in modern biology, though he added that it has to be tested carefully in each species.

Teo gave the idea a simple rule of thumb, which Maya copied onto the back of a paper bag. Helping tends to pay off, in evolutionary terms, when the benefit to a relative, reduced by how distant that relative is, outweighs the cost to the helper. A sister counts for four times as much as a first cousin in this sum, though the rule is a guide to what spreads and not a calculation that any animal makes.

Rosa wrapped a fresh loaf for her sister Carmen, and Maya laughed and asked whether she was doing the sum in her head. Rosa said that she was doing it out of love, and Teo agreed that the two explanations do not clash. The sum describes why such feelings could spread over the ages, but the feelings themselves are real, and nobody has to calculate anything to love a sister.

Ground squirrels sometimes give a loud alarm call when a hawk or a weasel approaches, which warns the others but may draw the predator's attention to the caller. In a long study, researchers found that females with relatives living nearby gave the alarm more often than females with none. This fits the idea that helping is more likely to spread when its benefits fall on family, although scientists continue to debate the details.

Maya studied the photographs again and said that family could not be the whole story, because her best friend at school was not a relative at all. Teo agreed that people and animals help friends and even strangers, and for different reasons. He promised that they would meet some astonishing examples before the summer was over, and that some of them would involve bats.

A mother bird flies back and forth all day to feed her hungry chicks, and she hardly stops to feed herself. Each chick carries about half of her gene versions, as it does for its father. Animals that care for their young therefore tend to leave more copies of the very genes that make them care, without any bird knowing why.

A pair of blue tits may make hundreds of trips in a single day to carry caterpillars to their hungry nestlings. Feeding a big brood is exhausting, and a parent that gives everything to this year's chicks may have too little strength left to survive and breed again. Natural selection therefore tends to favour parents that balance the needs of the present brood against their own chances in the future.

In a honeybee hive, thousands of workers never have young of their own, but spend their lives feeding and defending their mother, the queen. Because the workers share many genes with their sisters, biologists see this as one way that a trait can spread by helping relatives. They still argue, however, about how much relatedness explains it, and about what else may be involved.

Dario, who delivers the flour and keeps bees on a hill outside town, took Maya to see his hives one Saturday morning, and Teo came along. He explained that in honeybees the males hatch from unfertilised eggs and carry only one set of cards, so two sisters with the same father share about three quarters of their gene versions. Maya was delighted by this odd sum, and she watched the workers going in and out of the hive with new eyes.

The picture is not quite so simple, said Dario, because a honeybee queen mates with about a dozen drones before she settles into the hive. Most of the workers are therefore half sisters, who share much less than three quarters of their gene versions with one another. This is one reason why biologists argue about how far the odd arithmetic of bees really explains their way of life.

Helping is not always limited to relatives, because vampire bats will share blood from a meal with roost mates that failed to feed. Researchers have found that bats tend to help those that have helped them before. This shows that cooperation can also succeed when it is based on trust and repayment.

A vampire bat must feed almost every night, and one that goes hungry for two or three nights in a row may starve. A bat that has fed well can save a hungry neighbour by bringing up part of its blood meal and sharing it. Because the cost to the giver is small and the benefit to the receiver is enormous, the exchange can pay off for both sides over time.

Trading favours can only succeed when the same animals meet again and again, and when a selfish animal cannot simply take without giving. Vampire bats roost together for years, so they have plenty of chances to learn who helps them. A bat that never shares may therefore be less likely to be fed, which makes cheating a poor long-term plan.

Even in the closest families, the interests of the members can sometimes pull in different directions. A young mammal usually wants more milk and care than its mother is ready to give, because she must save strength for other offspring. The tug of war between them can be seen in many species, especially around weaning time.

On Sunday, Maya phoned her mother Elena, who was working far away for the summer, and told her all about the bees and the bats. Afterwards she told Teo that a family seemed to be both a team and a quarrel at the same time. Teo smiled and said that it was mostly a team, and that the quarrels were usually small ones that could be made up with a loaf of bread.

The common cuckoo lays its egg in the nest of a smaller bird, and the cuckoo chick that hatches soon pushes the other eggs out. The foster parents often work themselves to exhaustion feeding a chick that is much larger than they are. In some species, however, the hosts have evolved the ability to notice odd eggs, which in turn forces cuckoos to make better copies.

A female cuckoo watches from a tree until the owner of a nest has flown off, and then she slips in and out again in only a few seconds. In that short time she removes one of the host's eggs, lays an egg of her own and escapes before she can be caught. Her chick will then hatch a little earlier than the host's own chicks, which gives it a head start.

Many cuckoo eggs look astonishingly like the eggs of the bird being tricked, with the same background colour and the same pattern of speckles. A female cuckoo generally lays eggs that match just one kind of host, and the match has been improved over many generations, because hosts that spot a poor copy throw it out. Each generation of better forgeries descends from the ones that happened to get past the hosts' inspection.

A young cuckoo soon grows far too big for a reed warbler's nest, but it has one more trick, which is a special way of begging. Its rapid, urgent calls sound like those of a whole brood of hungry chicks, and so its foster parents keep bringing food at the rate that a full nest would demand. Scientists found this out by playing recordings of cuckoo calls and of warbler chick calls to nests, and watching how the parents behaved.

Every defence that a host evolves creates a reason for its parasites to evolve a way around it, and the same is true the other way round. This kind of contest never ends with a clear victor, because each new advantage is soon answered by the other side. Both sides must keep changing just to stay where they are, like runners on a moving track.

Biologists call this endless contest the Red Queen effect, after a character in Lewis Carroll's story Through the Looking-Glass. In the story, the Red Queen tells Alice that in her country you have to run as fast as you can just to stay in the same place. An American biologist named Leigh Van Valen suggested in 1973 that living things are in the same position, since each side must keep changing merely to avoid falling behind.

In the lakes of New Zealand, scientists studied a small snail that can reproduce either with a partner or on its own. In lakes where parasites were common, a larger share of the snails reproduced with partners, and where parasites were rare, the snails were more likely to go it alone. This fits the idea that mixing the cards helps to keep ahead of parasites, although no single study can settle such a big question.

In tropical forests, a fungus infects carpenter ants and somehow makes them climb a plant and clamp their jaws onto a leaf. The fungus then grows out of the dead ant and releases tiny spores, which drift down to infect more ants below. Scientists are still working out how the fungus controls the ant, and Teo used the case to show that the genes of one living thing can affect the behaviour of another.

Our own bodies take part in an arms race against germs, and they have been doing so for as long as there have been bodies. Some of the most varied genes in the whole human genome are those that help the immune system to recognise invaders, which makes it harder for any one germ to be ready for everybody. Flu viruses, meanwhile, change a little every year, which is why scientists must update the flu vaccine again and again.

Rosa found a spot of green mould on a forgotten loaf and wrinkled her nose, because mould and bakers have been rivals for as long as there has been bread. Maya wrote in her notebook that in nature nobody ever wins for good, since every new defence meets a new attack. Teo said that this was a fine sentence, and that a good scientist would try to find a place where it might be wrong.

It is tempting to think of genes as puppet strings, but the picture is wrong. Genes influence how the brain and body are built, and behaviour then arises from that body meeting the world around it. This means that the same genes can lead to very different lives, depending on what happens along the way.

Every morning the nurse Ines came into the bakery on her way home from the night shift, holding the hands of her nine-year-old twin sons, Leo and Nico. The two boys were identical, with the same freckles and the same crooked grins, and yet Leo always asked for a bun with raisins while Nico wanted plain bread. Maya had begun to wonder whether the difference was written in their cards or in something else entirely.

Identical twins begin life with almost exactly the same DNA, and yet even their fingerprints are different from each other. They have different friends, different hobbies and different habits, even when they grow up in the same house. This shows that the same instructions can produce distinct people once chance and experience have had their say.

Teo told Maya that twins differ for many small reasons that add up over the years. A few tiny mutations appear after the egg has split, and chance plays a part as each body grows, so even the position of each baby in the womb can matter. After birth, each boy meets different friends, tastes different foods and has different adventures, and all of these leave their mark.

Cells can add small chemical tags to DNA, and these work rather like pencil notes in the margin of a recipe card, saying use less of this or none of that. A tag can turn a gene up or down without changing a single letter, and the tags can be altered by what happens during a lifetime. Studies suggest that the tags of identical twins drift apart as they grow older, although scientists are still learning how much this matters.

Many people misread the term heritability, so Teo explained it slowly and with an example. A trait that is said to be fifty percent heritable does not mean that half of any one person is genetic. It means only that, in one particular group and setting, about half of the differences among people are linked to gene differences.

In many countries, the average adult is now taller than a great-grandparent was a hundred years ago, in some places by more than ten centimetres. The genes of a population cannot change very much in so short a time, but food, housing and health care improved enormously. Height is therefore a perfect example of a trait that is strongly influenced by genes and by the world at the same time.

Teo said that there is no single gene for being a baker, or for being kind, or for telling jokes. Behaviour is shaped by thousands of tiny nudges from the genes, together with everything that happens in a life, such as family, friends, luck and learning. A nudge is not a destiny, he added, because a gentle push in one direction can be cancelled by a push from somewhere else.

Teo gave an example of a gene that is not destiny, a rare condition called phenylketonuria, in which a baby cannot process one amino acid. Newborns are tested soon after birth with a tiny drop of blood from the heel. A special diet then prevents the damage, which shows that the effect of a gene can depend heavily on the environment.

That afternoon Maya shaped her first whole batch of rolls entirely on her own, while Rosa stood by and wisely said nothing. She told Teo that her genes had helped to give her these hands, but that she was the one who was learning what to do with them. Teo said that this was a very good way of putting it, and that it was close to the truth of the whole matter.

Teo told Maya that any two people on Earth have DNA that is almost exactly alike, differing by roughly one letter in a thousand. Most of those small differences exist within every large group of people, rather than between groups. The idea of sharply different human types therefore has no basis in our genes.

Our species is remarkably young, at only about three hundred thousand years old, which is a blink of the eye compared with the history of life. That has given evolution very little time to build up large differences between groups of people, and it is one reason why we are all so alike in our DNA. Teo added that chimpanzees hold more variety in their DNA than humans do, even though there are far fewer of them.

Our species began in Africa, and the groups who left that continent roughly sixty thousand years ago took only a part of its variety with them. For that reason, Africa still holds more genetic variety than any other region, and much of the variety found elsewhere is a smaller part of what exists there. Maya thought that this was an upside-down way of looking at the world, and Teo said that the best facts often are.

The features that people notice first, such as skin colour, depend largely on a small number of genes out of about twenty thousand. Skin colour has shifted over the ages with the strength of the sunlight in the places where families lived, so it reflects a long history of adaptation. It says almost nothing about the thousands of other genes that make a person who they are, which is why Teo called it skin-deep in the most literal sense.

Humans and chimpanzees share more than 98 out of every 100 DNA letters, which fits the idea that we had a common ancestor not very long ago in evolutionary terms. Most human genes also have a close counterpart in the mouse, a much more distant cousin of ours. Many have one in the fruit fly, which is why those animals are so useful in laboratories.

Teo drew a branching tree in the spilled flour, with a girl, a chimpanzee, a mouse, a fly and a yeast cell at the tips of the twigs. The more recently two branches split, he explained, the more alike their DNA tends to be, and humans and chimpanzees parted company only about six or seven million years ago. Yeast branched off from our line far earlier, over a billion years ago, and so we share far fewer of its cards.

A tiny worm that lives in the soil, and is no longer than a millimetre, has about as many genes as a person does. Rice has even more, so the number of genes cannot be what decides how complicated a living thing is. The difference lies in how the cards are used, such as when they are switched on, in which cells, and in what combinations.

To find out what a gene does, scientists often disable it in a fly, a worm or a mouse and watch what changes. Because so many of the old cards are shared, they can then look for the human version of the gene in people who have a related problem. Teo added that the work is done under strict rules for the care of animals, and that it has helped to explain many illnesses.

Bacteria have a trick that most animals lack, because they can pass small loops of DNA called plasmids from one cell to another, even between different kinds of bacteria. A gene for resisting a medicine can therefore spread sideways through a crowd, and not only from parent to child. This makes the lower branches of the tree of life look less like a tree and more like a tangled net.

Maya looked at the tree in the flour for a long time, and then she wrote the word cousin beside every tip of every twig. Everything alive, from the yeast in the dough to the girl who kneaded it, belonged to a single enormous family that was billions of years old. She felt oddly cheered by the thought, and she noticed that she could not look at a bowl of dough in quite the same way again.

Dogs descend from wolves that began living alongside people many thousands of years ago. Humans kept breeding the animals with the traits they liked, such as gentleness, speed or a good nose. Over time this choice changed gene versions so much that a tiny terrier and a huge hound can both belong to the same species.

In 1959 a scientist named Dmitri Belyaev began an experiment with silver foxes on a farm in Siberia. Each generation he allowed only the tamest foxes to breed, and within about ten generations some of the pups were wagging their tails and seeking human company. As the experiment went on, many of the foxes also developed floppy ears and spotted coats, which suggests that the genes for tameness are linked with other features in ways that nobody had expected.

Cabbage, kale, broccoli and cauliflower all belong to a single species, which began as a wild plant growing on the seaside cliffs of western Europe. Farmers saved seeds from plants with bigger leaves, thicker buds or fatter flower heads, and over many centuries these choices shaped a handful of quite different vegetables. Teo said that the next time Maya ate her broccoli, she should remember that she was eating the result of a very long selection experiment.

Maize, the grain that fills tortillas and cornflakes, was shaped from a small wild grass called teosinte in what is now Mexico about nine thousand years ago. Farmers saved seeds from the plants they liked best, season after season, without knowing anything about genes. Across hundreds of generations they changed the gene versions of the whole crop, until it hardly resembled its wild ancestor.

Rosa's flour comes from bread wheat, a plant whose genome is about five times larger than the human genome. It has six sets of seven chromosomes, forty-two in all, because it arose when three different wild grasses combined their cards in one plant. Dario, who delivers the flour, said that he had never imagined a sack of flour might hold such a tangled family history.

In 2012, scientists described a tool called CRISPR, which can cut and change DNA at a chosen place, a little like a find and replace command for genes. In 2023, the first treatment based on it was approved for sickle cell disease, bringing hope to many patients and their families. The technology also raises serious ethical questions, however, which societies are still debating today.

CRISPR began as a kind of defence that bacteria use against viruses, long before anyone had noticed it. Scientists learned to give the cutting protein a short guide strand that matches one chosen place in the DNA, so that the cut is made exactly there and, if all goes well, nowhere else. The cell then repairs the break, and that repair is the moment when a letter can be changed, removed or replaced.

The new treatment takes blood-making cells from a patient and edits them so that they make the kind of haemoglobin that babies use before birth, which does not bend into sickle shapes. The edited cells are then returned to the patient, who needs intensive hospital care before and after the procedure. Teo said that this was a wonderful step, and that the great challenge now is to make such treatments affordable for the many people who need them.

Changing the cells of one patient affects only that person, but a change made in an egg, a sperm cell or an early embryo would be inherited by the children and grandchildren who followed. For that reason many countries have strict rules, or outright bans, on editing of that kind, and scientists keep debating questions of safety, fairness and consent. Teo said that these are not questions for scientists alone, because they belong to everybody.

The first reading of a human genome was finished in 2003 after many years of work by teams around the world, and it cost billions of dollars. Today the same job can be done in a day or two, using machines that scan millions of fragments at once. It now costs only a small fraction as much, a change that has transformed medicine and research.

Most results of a gene test are expressed as chances rather than promises, because so many genes, and so much of life, influence what happens. Teo said that anyone who gets such a result should talk to a doctor or a genetic counsellor. Such a professional can explain what the result does and does not mean for that particular person.

Because relatives share gene versions, one person's test can also reveal something about brothers, sisters, parents and cousins, who never took the test. For that reason privacy matters a great deal, and people should be able to decide for themselves who sees their results. Teo said that clear laws, honest advice and kindness are as important to the future of genetics as clever machines.

Teo said that explaining why something happens is not the same as saying it is good. The process of evolution has no moral purpose, so the fact that a behaviour is natural gives us no reason to excuse it. We are free to choose kindness, fairness and care, whatever our ancestors may have done.

Rosa put on her glasses to read a faded card, and Teo smiled at the sight. Glasses, vaccines and medicines all go against what nature would do if it were left alone, and almost nobody thinks that they are wrong. The question that matters, he said, is never whether something is natural but whether it is kind, fair and wise.

Maya realised that Rosa's recipes were not the only things that had been passed on in her family, since there were songs, stories, habits and sayings too. Humans hand down their language, skills and customs by teaching one another rather than through DNA. These cultural inheritances change much faster than genes and often matter just as much.

Humans are not the only animals that pass on things that they have learned, and Maya was glad to hear it. Humpback whales pass new songs from one group to the next across the vast Pacific Ocean, and young birds of many kinds learn their songs largely from adults. Teo said that learning handed down by imitation is a second kind of inheritance, running alongside the first, and that it is especially powerful in our own species.

Teo pointed out something that made Maya pause, which was that each of her genes had been copied, again and again, through an unbroken line of ancestors. Every one of those ancestors had lived long enough to have young of their own. The chain of copies reaches back across billions of years to the very first living cells.

You have two parents, four grandparents and eight great-grandparents, and on paper the number doubles with every generation. Thirty generations back, which is only about eight hundred years ago, the sum comes to more than a billion ancestors, far more people than were alive at the time. The answer is that the same people appear again and again on the tree, and so all of us are distant cousins of one another many times over.

On the final Saturday of the summer, Rosa gave a party in the bakery for all her neighbours, and Ines, the twins, Dario and Carmen were there. Teo asked Maya one last question, which was what a gene really is, and the whole room fell silent to hear her reply. Maya stood up and answered that a gene is a recipe that is copied, read by tiny workers and tested in a living body, and that it never wants anything and never works alone.

On the last evening of the summer, Maya wrote her own recipe for a new kind of bread and slid it into the box beside her grandmother's cards. Teo said that she was a new edition of a very old book, copied with care and changed a little. She would help to write the next page, he said, and the book was still unfinished.
